section: The question that organizes this book
text:
The question that organizes this book
An isolated quantum state evolves reversibly. A cup of coffee cools irreversibly. How can the second statement emerge from the first? This book develops the answer through observables, energy eigenstates, dephasing, conservation laws, and controlled approximations. The central bridge is the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, or ETH: in suitable interacting systems, individual energy eigenstates already encode thermal predictions for simple observables.
This is an independent course companion to the review by Luca D’Alessio, Yariv Kafri, Anatoli Polkovnikov, and Marcos Rigol  [1]. Its topic sequence supplies our backbone. The explanations, worked calculations, exercises, code, and figures here are original. This is neither an edition of the review nor a claim that its authors endorse the book. Read the original review for its historical synthesis and extensive literature survey.

title: Quantum Chaos to Thermodynamics
text:
Who this is for
You should know vectors, matrices, derivatives, elementary probability, and the Schrödinger equation. Chapter 1 develops the density matrix, partial trace, entropy, and the ensembles used later. No prior course in quantum chaos or nonequilibrium statistical mechanics is assumed. Keep a notebook: reproducing a short derivation usually teaches more than reading a long one.
The book moves from classical chaos and random matrices to many-body eigenstates and quenches; then from population dynamics to entropy, work fluctuations, response, and heating; finally to integrability, generalized ensembles, and prethermalization. The mathematical appendix supplies the auxiliary proofs, while the numerical lab makes the principal diagnostics reproducible in Julia. A section-by-section coverage map includes every numbered subsection and appendix of the review.

section: Conventions and the strength of claims
text:
Conventions and the strength of claims
We use \(k_B=1\) unless restored explicitly, so entropy is dimensionless and inverse temperature is \(\beta=1/T\). Chapters may set \(\hbar=1\) for a calculation and say so. \(N\) counts particles or sites, \(D\) is a Hilbert-space dimension, and \(S(E)=\ln[\rho(E)\delta E]\) is a shell entropy; the reference window \(\delta E\) must be specified when an absolute entropy matters. An observable is a Hermitian operator. “Local” means supported on a bounded number of nearby sites as the total system grows.
Three types of statements recur:

Exact statements follow from linear algebra, unitary dynamics, or explicitly stated probability assumptions. Examples are conservation of von Neumann entropy under unitary evolution and the two-measurement Jarzynski identity for a Gibbs initial state.
Conditional results follow once assumptions such as ETH, nondegenerate energy gaps, local equilibration, weak driving, or a Markov approximation hold. The assumptions belong to the result.
Numerical observations and conjectures include Wigner–Dyson behavior in many physical models, strong ETH in generic systems, and the random-matrix description of zeta zeros. Finite-size plots do not turn these into theorems.

Thermalization concerns a chosen class of observables and a stated time window. It does not mean that a pure global state becomes a mixed global Gibbs state. Spectral chaos, entanglement, equilibration, and transport are related diagnostics with distinct definitions. The chapters develop those distinctions before using them.

title: 1  States, observables, and equilibrium ensembles
text:
1.1 The quantum state as a prediction rule
A gas in a sealed box obeys reversible microscopic equations. Nevertheless, its pressure becomes predictable without knowing every particle’s position or every amplitude of its wavefunction. The central question of this book is how a small set of observables can become insensitive to most microscopic information. We begin by defining exactly which information an observable accesses and what an equilibrium prediction means.
A normalized vector \(\ket{\psi}\) describes a pure state. The probability of obtaining the result \(a\) when measuring \(A=\sum_a aP_a\) is \(\bra{\psi}P_a\ket{\psi}\). A density matrix packages both pure and mixed preparations:
\[
\rho=\sum_j p_j\ket{\psi_j}\bra{\psi_j},\qquad
p_j\geq0,\qquad\sum_jp_j=1,\qquad
\langle A\rangle_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A).
\tag{1.1}\]
A density matrix is positive, Hermitian, and has unit trace. Its decomposition into preparation vectors is generally not unique; predictions depend on \(\rho\), not on a chosen decomposition. Purity, \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2\), equals one for a pure state and is smaller for a mixed state. The von Neumann entropy, in units with \(k_{\mathrm B}=1\), is
\[
S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\ln\rho).
\tag{1.2}\]
Zero eigenvalues contribute zero because \(x\ln x\to0\) as \(x\to0^+\). Unitary evolution, \(\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U^\dagger(t)\), preserves every eigenvalue of \(\rho\), hence preserves this entropy. An isolated pure state therefore never becomes a mixed Gibbs state as a statement about its full density matrix.
Why, then, can a subsystem become thermal? For \(\mathcal H=\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_B\), the reduced state is \(\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho\). In bases \(\ket{a}\ket{b}\),
\[
(\rho_A)_{aa'}=\sum_b\rho_{ab,a'b},\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A\otimes I_B)=\operatorname{Tr}_A(\rho_A A).
\tag{1.3}\]
For the entangled vector \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), the global entropy is zero but \(\rho_A=I_A/2\) has entropy \(\ln2\). Entanglement allows local ignorance within a completely specified global state. No averaging over an observer’s ignorance is needed for this example.

title: 1  States, observables, and equilibrium ensembles
text:
1.2 Three ensembles and their assumptions
Suppose energy is the only extensive conserved quantity besides fixed particle number and volume. An isolated equilibrium system with energy known within a window \(\mathcal W=[E-\Delta/2,E+\Delta/2]\) is assigned
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{mc}}=\frac{P_{\mathcal W}}{D_{\mathcal W}},\qquad
P_{\mathcal W}=\sum_{E_n\in\mathcal W}\ket n\bra n,\qquad
D_{\mathcal W}=\operatorname{Tr}P_{\mathcal W}.
\tag{1.4}\]
The window should contain many levels while remaining narrow on the energy scale over which the target observable changes appreciably. The microcanonical prescription is a prediction rule whose dynamical justification remains to be established; it is not an extra term in the Schrödinger equation.
For a system exchanging energy with a large reservoir, the canonical state is
\[
\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z},\qquad Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H},\qquad\beta=1/T.
\tag{1.5}\]
If particles can also be exchanged, \(\rho_{\beta,\mu}=e^{-\beta(H-\mu N)}/\mathcal Z\), provided \([H,N]=0\). Other exact charges require corresponding constraints. Throughout this book, comparing states from different conserved-charge sectors without specifying their weights is an avoidable source of confusion.
Here is a derivation of the Boltzmann factor. Let \(H=H_A+H_B+H_{AB}\) and initially neglect the boundary interaction when counting levels. If \(A\) has energy \(\epsilon_a\), the number of compatible reservoir states is \(\Omega_B(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-\epsilon_a)\). Therefore
\[
p_a\propto e^{S_B(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-\epsilon_a)}
\simeq e^{S_B(E_{\mathrm{tot}})-\beta\epsilon_a},\qquad
\beta=\left.\frac{\partial S_B}{\partial E_B}\right|_{E_{\mathrm{tot}}}.
\tag{1.6}\]
The next term is \(-\epsilon_a^2/(2T^2C_B)\) after choosing a suitable reference energy. A reservoir of large heat capacity suppresses this correction. The approximation also requires a coupling weak enough that the subsystem energy remains meaningful. At appreciable coupling, the reduced equilibrium state need not be \(e^{-\beta H_A}/Z_A\) for the bare subsystem Hamiltonian.
The same canonical distribution follows by maximizing \(-\sum_np_n\ln p_n\) with fixed normalization and mean energy. A variation gives \(\ln p_n=-1-\alpha-\beta E_n\). This is a useful inference principle, but maximizing entropy by itself does not prove that a particular Hamiltonian carries an arbitrary preparation to that distribution.

section: 1.3 Thermodynamic functions from a partition function
text:
1.3 Thermodynamic functions from a partition function
Differentiating the finite-dimensional partition function gives exact identities:
\[
U=-\partial_\beta\ln Z,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_\beta(H)=\partial_\beta^2\ln Z,
\qquad C=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_\beta(H)}{T^2}.
\tag{1.7}\]
For finite-range systems away from a critical point, both \(U\) and \(C\) usually scale as the number of sites \(L\). Thus the energy width scales as \(\sqrt L\) while the mean energy is extensive. The width in energy density, \(\Delta e=\Delta E/L\), vanishes as \(L^{-1/2}\). This is the scale separation behind much ensemble equivalence.
More explicitly, write the number of states near \(E=Le\) as \(\exp[Ls(e)+o(L)]\). The canonical sum is approximated by
\[
Z(\beta)\approx\int \mathrm de\,\exp\{L[s(e)-\beta e]\}.
\tag{1.8}\]
If \(s(e)\) is smooth and strictly concave near a unique maximum of \(s(e)-\beta e\), a saddle point gives \(s'(e_*)=\beta\) and a narrow distribution around \(e_*\). A local observable smooth in \(e\) then has the same leading prediction in microcanonical and canonical ensembles. This argument assumes the thermodynamic limit and thermodynamic stability. Long-range interactions, first-order coexistence, and nonconcave entropy can obstruct simple versions of equivalence. Even when local observables agree, the global density matrices and energy fluctuations can differ greatly.
For \(L\) independent two-level systems with energies \(0\) and \(\epsilon\), \(Z=(1+e^{-\beta\epsilon})^L\) and the excited fraction is \(q=(1+e^{\beta\epsilon})^{-1}\). The microcanonical count with \(M=Lq\) excitations is \(\binom LM\). Stirling’s formula gives \(s(q)=-q\ln q-(1-q)\ln(1-q)\), so \(\partial S/\partial E=\epsilon^{-1}\ln[(1-q)/q]\), recovering the same temperature. This solvable counting problem illustrates ensemble equivalence without assuming chaos.

title: 1  States, observables, and equilibrium ensembles
section: 1.4 Typicality: a kinematic fact with a dynamical limitation
text:
1.4 Typicality: a kinematic fact with a dynamical limitation
Let a constrained subspace \(\mathcal H_R\) have dimension \(D_R\) and define \(\Omega=P_R/D_R\). Choose a unit vector uniformly with the unitary invariant Haar measure in this subspace. For an observable \(A_R=P_RAP_R\),
\[
\mathbb E\langle A\rangle_\psi=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_R A_R}{D_R},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\langle A\rangle_\psi)=
\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_R(A_R^2)/D_R-[\operatorname{Tr}_R A_R/D_R]^2}{D_R+1}.
\tag{1.9}\]
One obtains this by using \(\mathbb E[(\ket\psi\bra\psi)^{\otimes2}]=(I+\mathsf F)/[D_R(D_R+1)]\), where \(\mathsf F\) swaps two copies of the subspace. The variance is at most \(\|A\|^2/(D_R+1)\). Most vectors therefore give nearly the same answer for any fixed bounded observable when \(D_R\) is large. The canonical-typicality results of  [1] establish corresponding closeness statements for a sufficiently small subsystem under appropriate dimension conditions; see also  [2] for the energy-shell formulation.
This is a statement about measure on a space of vectors. A time-independent Hamiltonian keeps the absolute values of its energy-basis coefficients fixed, so a physical orbit never samples all Haar-random vectors. Moreover, easily prepared low-entanglement states are atypical. Typicality explains why thermal-looking pure states are abundant; it leaves open whether physical dynamics reaches them, and how quickly. Those questions motivate quantum chaos and ETH.






NoteWhat does “thermal” mean here?



Specify an observable class and an accuracy. A subsystem is thermal when its reduced state is close enough to an equilibrium state to reproduce that class. Equilibration means small deviations from a stationary value for most times. Thermalization additionally identifies that value with an equilibrium ensemble fixed by the conserved macroscopic data.

title: 1  States, observables, and equilibrium ensembles
text:
1.5 Exercises and worked answers
1. Entropy without mixing. For \(\ket\psi=\sqrt p\ket{00}+\sqrt{1-p}\ket{11}\), calculate the purity and entropy of \(A\).






TipAnswer





Tracing \(B\) removes the cross terms: \(\rho_A=\operatorname{diag}(p,1-p)\). Therefore \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2=p^2+(1-p)^2\) and \(S_A=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p)\). The global state remains pure for every \(p\).



2. Finite reservoir correction. Show that \(S_B''(E_B)=-1/(T^2C_B)\) and identify when the quadratic correction in Equation 1.6 matters.






TipAnswer





Differentiate \(S_B'=1/T\): \(S_B''=-(1/T^2)(\partial T/\partial E_B)=-1/(T^2C_B)\). Expanding around the mean subsystem energy gives a correction of order \((\epsilon_a-\bar\epsilon)^2/(T^2C_B)\). It is small when the reservoir heat capacity greatly exceeds the subsystem energy-variance scale measured in units of \(T^2\).



3. A zero-temperature caveat. Why does the saddle-point argument not automatically justify a canonical description of an arbitrary low-energy pure state?






TipAnswer





It compares equilibrium ensembles under smoothness and large-deviation assumptions. It says nothing about a pure state’s overlaps with eigenstates. Near a spectral edge, the number of participating levels may be small and the entropy expansion can fail. Dynamical thermalization requires additional information about the eigenstates and the preparation.

title: 2  Classical mechanics: regular motion, ergodicity, and chaos
text:
2.1 Hamiltonian flow preserves volume
Classical chaos provides an instructive route from microscopic trajectories to equilibrium averages. It also provides warnings: instability of trajectories, exploration of an energy surface, and relaxation of an observable are different mathematical properties. We separate them before asking what survives quantization.
For \(f\) canonical coordinate-momentum pairs, let \(z=(q_1,\ldots,q_f,p_1,\ldots,p_f)\). Hamilton’s equations are \(\dot q_i=\partial H/\partial p_i\) and \(\dot p_i=-\partial H/\partial q_i\). The Poisson bracket,
\[
\{A,B\}=\sum_i\left(
\frac{\partial A}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial B}{\partial p_i}
-\frac{\partial A}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial B}{\partial q_i}\right),
\qquad\frac{\mathrm d A}{\mathrm dt}=\{A,H\}
\tag{2.1}\]
for an observable without explicit time dependence, makes conserved quantities transparent: \(I\) is conserved if \(\{I,H\}=0\).
The divergence of the phase-space velocity vanishes because mixed derivatives cancel:
\[
\nabla_z\cdot\dot z=\sum_i\left(
\frac{\partial^2H}{\partial q_i\partial p_i}
-\frac{\partial^2H}{\partial p_i\partial q_i}\right)=0.
\tag{2.2}\]
A transported probability density consequently obeys Liouville’s equation, \(\partial_t\rho+\{\rho,H\}=0\). Along each trajectory \(\rho\) is constant. The fine-grained Gibbs entropy \(-\int\rho\ln\rho\,\mathrm dz\) is conserved. Classical relaxation therefore cannot mean that the exact density is crushed onto a thermal attractor in phase space. Hamiltonian systems have no dissipative attractor of that kind.
For bounded motion, the normalized microcanonical measure is
\[
\mathrm d\mu_E(z)=\frac{\delta(E-H(z))\,\mathrm dz}
{\int\delta(E-H(z))\,\mathrm dz}.
\tag{2.3}\]
The delta function includes a geometric weight: in coordinates on the energy surface it is the area element divided by \(|\nabla H|\). Uniform measure on a plotted surface is therefore not automatically the microcanonical measure. A trajectory spends more time where it moves slowly.

title: 2  Classical mechanics: regular motion, ergodicity, and chaos
text:
2.2 Integrability and action-angle coordinates
A system with \(f\) independent conserved quantities in involution, \(\{I_i,I_j\}=0\), is Liouville integrable under suitable regularity assumptions. A compact, connected, regular common level set of these quantities is an \(f\)-dimensional torus. The action variables are
\[
I_i=\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_{\gamma_i}\sum_jp_j\,\mathrm dq_j,
\qquad
H=H(I),\qquad
\dot I_i=0,\qquad\dot\theta_i=\omega_i(I).
\tag{2.4}\]
Each angle is periodic modulo \(2\pi\). Thus \(\theta_i(t)=\theta_i(0)+\omega_it\). A trajectory can densely fill a torus when its frequencies are rationally independent, but this torus has dimension \(f\), smaller than the \(2f-1\) energy surface for \(f>1\). Being dense on the accessible invariant torus does not imply energy-surface ergodicity.
For two uncoupled oscillators, \(H=\omega_1I_1+\omega_2I_2\). Fixing total energy still leaves the energy division between oscillators undetermined. If the first oscillator initially carries nearly all the energy, it keeps that energy. A microcanonical average over all divisions cannot describe every trajectory. This simple failure is the classical precursor of the need for additional charges in integrable quantum systems.
Weakly coupling an integrable system does not immediately destroy all invariant tori. For nondegenerate systems and sufficiently small smooth perturbations, KAM theory guarantees persistence of a set of nonresonant tori. Near resonances the dynamics can instead form islands, separatrices, and chaotic regions. A realistic phase portrait may therefore be mixed. A single parameter does not turn every region of phase space from regular to chaotic at the same moment.

title: 2  Classical mechanics: regular motion, ergodicity, and chaos
text:
2.3 Ergodicity, mixing, and observable relaxation
A measure-preserving flow \(\Phi^t\) is ergodic when invariant sets have measure zero or one. Equivalently, for suitable observables and almost every initial point,
\[
\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\frac1\tau\int_0^\tau
A(\Phi^tz)\,\mathrm dt=\int A\,\mathrm d\mu_E.
\tag{2.5}\]
“Almost every” excludes sets of measure zero and says nothing about how fast the average converges. Ergodicity is a statement about infinite-time averages, while an experiment observes finite-time behavior.
Mixing is stronger. For square-integrable observables it requires decay of connected correlations:
\[
C_{AB}(t)=\int A(\Phi^tz)B(z)\,\mathrm d\mu_E
-\left(\int A\,\mathrm d\mu_E\right)
\left(\int B\,\mathrm d\mu_E\right)\longrightarrow0.
\tag{2.6}\]
An initial density of the form \(\rho_0=(1+\epsilon B)\rho_{\mathrm{mc}}\), with \(\int B\,\mathrm d\mu_E=0\), gives \(\langle A(t)\rangle-\langle A\rangle_{\mathrm{mc}}=\epsilon C_{AB}(t)\). This identity connects a statistical property of the equilibrium flow with relaxation of a weak perturbation. A stretched and folded density can become indistinguishable from equilibrium to a smooth observable even though its fine-grained entropy is unchanged.
A useful exactly solvable example is free motion on a circle, \(\theta(t)=\theta_0+\omega t\). Continuous-time averages equal the uniform angular average for \(\omega\ne0\). Yet \(A=e^{i\theta}\) has a correlation proportional to \(e^{i\omega t}\), whose magnitude never decays. The motion is ergodic on the circle under the continuous flow but is not mixing. This example prevents conflating an average with relaxation.

title: 2  Classical mechanics: regular motion, ergodicity, and chaos
text:
2.4 Instability and Lyapunov exponents
For nearby initial conditions, linearize Hamilton’s equations:
\[
\delta\dot z=J\,H''(z(t))\delta z,\qquad
\lambda=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t
\ln\frac{\|\delta z(t)\|}{\|\delta z(0)\|},
\quad
J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{2.7}\]
The limit is taken for infinitesimal perturbations with appropriate repeated rescaling; two finite trajectories cannot separate exponentially forever in a bounded region. A positive maximal exponent characterizes exponential sensitivity in typical chaotic trajectories. Symplectic dynamics pairs exponents as \(+\lambda\) and \(-\lambda\), preserving phase-space volume. Autonomous Hamiltonian flows also have zero exponents associated with flow and energy conservation in the usual nonsingular setting.
An inverted oscillator has exponential instability, but its unbounded escape is not the equilibrium chaos of a confined gas. Conversely, global transport can be slow in a chaotic region because narrow passages and approximate conservation laws restrict motion. A Lyapunov time measures loss of trajectory predictability; it need not equal the thermalization time.
For the area-preserving standard map,
\[
p_{n+1}=p_n+K\sin\theta_n,\qquad
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+p_{n+1}\pmod{2\pi},
\tag{2.8}\]
the Jacobian has determinant one. Small \(K\) leaves extensive regular structures; larger \(K\) produces substantial chaotic regions. The map is a convenient teaching model of stretching and transport, but claims about its global ergodicity need careful parameter and phase-space qualifications.






Figure 2.1: Original phase portraits of the standard map at \(K=0.2\) and \(K=5\). Nine initial conditions are iterated for 1,800 steps; the displayed momentum is reduced modulo \(2\pi\), giving a torus portrait. Regular islands and chaotic-looking regions can coexist. The code and preparation are documented in the numerical laboratory.

title: 2  Classical mechanics: regular motion, ergodicity, and chaos
text:
2.5 Coarse observations and reversible dynamics
Partition phase space into cells and retain only the probability in each cell. Stretching and folding can move a smooth initial distribution into narrow filaments crossing many cells. Cell averages then lose access to the detailed filaments. The entropy of that coarse description can increase while the fine-grained entropy remains constant. Its value depends on the resolution, and it need not increase monotonically for every initial distribution.
Reversing every momentum can retrace a time-reversal-invariant trajectory. Such a reversal also reconstructs the fine correlations needed to reverse the apparent entropy increase. This observation locates the origin of the arrow of relaxation in a special low-correlation preparation and restricted observations, together with dynamics that distributes information over inaccessible scales. It does not license replacing Hamilton’s equations by irreversible evolution at the microscopic level.

title: 2  Classical mechanics: regular motion, ergodicity, and chaos
text:
2.6 Quantization changes the diagnostic
Semiclassical quantization of a regular torus gives, schematically, \(I_i=\hbar(n_i+\alpha_i/4)\), where \(\alpha_i\) is a Maslov index determined by turning points. Independent actions produce families of quantum numbers. In contrast, an ergodic classical orbit has no such global action labeling.
Two important proposals connect these structures to quantum spectra: generic integrable systems tend toward Poisson level statistics in the semiclassical limit  [1], while fully chaotic systems tend toward the appropriate random-matrix statistics after resolving symmetries  [2]. These are semiclassical universality proposals with assumptions and exceptions, not theorems covering every Hamiltonian. Arithmetic symmetries, degeneracies, mixed phase space, and the choice of limit matter.
Unitary dynamics preserves the overlap between two state vectors: \(\langle\psi(t)|\phi(t)\rangle=\langle\psi(0)|\phi(0)\rangle\). Thus the classical definition based directly on exponentially separating state vectors cannot simply be copied. Quantum chaos instead uses spectra, eigenfunctions, matrix elements, and dynamical probes. The next chapter develops the spectral route.

title: 2  Classical mechanics: regular motion, ergodicity, and chaos
text:
2.7 Exercises and worked answers
1. Volume preservation. Verify that the standard map preserves area even though it can amplify a small perturbation.






TipAnswer





Using input ordering \((\theta,p)\), the Jacobian is \(\begin{pmatrix}1+K\cos\theta&1\\K\cos\theta&1\end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is one. An expanding direction can coexist with a contracting direction of reciprocal stretching factor. Area preservation does not bound the largest singular value by one.



2. An integrable microcanonical mismatch. For two identical harmonic oscillators at total energy \(E\), compare the long-time value of the first oscillator’s energy with the microcanonical prediction.






TipAnswer





The trajectory preserves \(E_1\), so its time average is the initially chosen \(E_1\). Exchange symmetry gives \(\langle E_1\rangle_{\mathrm{mc}}=E/2\). The two agree only for a special energy division. Each invariant torus retains information absent from the energy-only ensemble.



3. Correlation versus average. Show explicitly why uniform rotation is not mixing.






TipAnswer





With uniform measure and \(A=e^{i\theta}\), \(B=e^{-i\theta}\), both individual averages vanish. Their correlation is \(\int e^{i(\theta+\omega t)}e^{-i\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta/(2\pi)=e^{i\omega t}\). It does not tend to zero, even though the time average of each nonzero Fourier harmonic vanishes.







[1] M. V. Berry and M. Tabor, Level clustering in the regular spectrum, Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A 356, 375 (1977).


[2] O. Bohigas, M. J. Giannoni, and C. Schmit, Characterization of chaotic quantum spectra and universality of level fluctuation laws, Physical Review Letters 52, 1 (1984).

title: 3  Random matrices and the fingerprints of quantum chaos
text:
3.1 The three Gaussian ensembles
A many-body Hamiltonian is highly structured: interactions are local, charges are conserved, and its entries are not independent random numbers. Random-matrix theory is useful because some fluctuations can forget that detailed structure. The aim is to identify which fluctuations are universal, after choosing the correct energy window and symmetry sector.
A Hermitian matrix can be diagonalized as \(H=UEU^\dagger\). Gaussian invariant ensembles assign a probability density of the form \(P(H)\propto e^{-c\operatorname{Tr}H^2}\), with \(c\) setting the energy scale. Invariance under basis rotations makes eigenvector orientations uniform and independent of the eigenvalues. The relevant rotation group depends on antiunitary symmetry:
The Dyson index is unrelated to inverse temperature. A physical time-reversal operator can exchange symmetry sectors instead of acting within one. Classification must therefore be done after the Hamiltonian is decomposed into irreducible symmetry blocks. Merely inspecting whether some terms look complex in a chosen basis is insufficient.
Changing variables from matrix entries to eigenvalues and eigenvectors produces a Jacobian:
\[
P(E_1,\ldots,E_D)\propto
\exp\left[-c\sum_nE_n^2\right]
\prod_{m<n}|E_m-E_n|^{\beta_{\mathrm D}}.
\tag{3.1}\]
To see the origin of the product, make an infinitesimal change of eigenbasis, with \(\dd K=U^\dagger\dd U\). In that basis, \(U^\dagger\dd H U=\dd E+[\dd K,E]\), so an off-diagonal variation has magnitude \(|E_m-E_n|\,|\dd K_{mn}|\). Each pair has one independent real component for GOE, two for GUE, and four for GSE after accounting for Kramers structure. The change of volume element therefore contributes one, two, or four powers of the gap for each pair. Invariance makes the remaining angular measure independent of \(E\).
The product suppresses nearby eigenvalues. It can also be read as a logarithmically repelling gas confined by a quadratic potential. This effective gas is a probability model of spectra, not a claim that energy levels exert physical forces.

section: 3.2 Level repulsion from a two-dimensional calculation
text:
3.2 Level repulsion from a two-dimensional calculation
Consider a real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrix,
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix},\qquad
E_+-E_-=2\sqrt{[(a-c)/2]^2+b^2}.
\tag{3.2}\]
GOE variances make \(x=(a-c)/2\) and \(y=b\) identically distributed independent Gaussians. In polar coordinates, the area element is \(r\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\phi\). Consequently the gap density is proportional to the gap near zero. After normalizing the mean gap to one, the result is the Wigner surmise,
\[
P_{\mathrm{GOE}}(s)=\frac\pi2s\,e^{-\pi s^2/4},\qquad
P_{\mathrm{GUE}}(s)=\frac{32}{\pi^2}s^2e^{-4s^2/\pi}.
\tag{3.3}\]
The GUE has three independent components controlling the gap, giving a volume element proportional to \(r^2\mathrm dr\). GSE has repulsion \(P(s)\propto s^4\) at small spacing. The two-level formulas approximate large-matrix nearest-neighbor statistics very accurately but are not the exact large-\(D\) spacing laws.
For independent unfolded levels, the probability that an interval of length \(s\) contains no level is \(e^{-s}\). Differentiating gives \(P_{\mathrm P}(s)=e^{-s}\). Unlike GOE or GUE statistics, this Poisson process permits arbitrarily small spacings with finite probability density.






Figure 3.1: Original comparison of exact Poisson samples with 25 independently sampled GOE matrices of dimension 350, retaining the central 60 percent of each spectrum and unfolding with the semicircle density. The GOE curve is the Wigner surmise. Sampling and unfolding choices are documented in the numerical laboratory.

title: 3  Random matrices and the fingerprints of quantum chaos
text:
3.3 Unfolding and symmetry resolution
A spectrum generally has an energy-dependent mean density \(\bar\rho(E)\). Define the smooth integrated counting function \(\bar N(E)=\int^E\bar\rho(E')\,\mathrm dE'\) and unfolded levels \(x_n=\bar N(E_n)\). Their mean spacing is approximately one. Using raw spacings across a broad band confuses the smooth density of states with fluctuations. Conversely, fitting the staircase too closely can remove the correlations one wants to measure.
Adjacent-gap ratios reduce this sensitivity:
\[
\delta_n=E_{n+1}-E_n,\qquad
r_n=\frac{\min(\delta_n,\delta_{n+1})}
{\max(\delta_n,\delta_{n+1})}\in[0,1].
\tag{3.4}\]
A slowly varying local density cancels between adjacent gaps. For independent exponential gaps the density is \(P(r)=2/(1+r)^2\), giving \(\langle r\rangle=2\ln2-1\). GOE spectra instead have a larger mean, close to \(0.53\).  [1] developed accurate random-matrix ratio distributions. Ratios still require symmetry resolution and an energy window: a sharp change of density over a few gaps can spoil the cancellation.
Independent symmetry sectors can cross without repulsion. Combining them produces excess small spacings even when each sector separately has GOE statistics. A correct numerical workflow first fixes particle number, momentum when translation applies, parity where compatible, and any additional exact charge. At special momenta, extra spatial symmetries often survive.
A further distinction is between the mean density and fluctuations around it. With entries normalized so that off-diagonal variance is \(v^2/D\), the large-\(D\) Gaussian ensembles have the semicircle density
\[
\bar\rho(E)=\frac{D}{2\pi v^2}\sqrt{4v^2-E^2},\qquad |E|<2v.
\tag{3.5}\]
Its integral is \(D\), so it counts levels rather than probabilities. Many physical local Hamiltonians instead have an approximately Gaussian bulk density, reflecting sums of numerous local energy contributions. Agreement with GOE fluctuations does not require a semicircular physical density: unfolding removes that smooth profile. The figure uses semicircle unfolding because its matrices are themselves sampled from GOE. A physical-chain calculation requires a suitable smooth density for that chain.

title: 3  Random matrices and the fingerprints of quantum chaos
text:
3.4 Eigenvectors and matrix elements
For a uniformly distributed real unit vector with components \(u_i\),
\[
\mathbb E u_i^2=\frac1D,\qquad
\mathbb E u_i^4=\frac{3}{D(D+2)}.
\tag{3.6}\]
Thus a single component is approximately Gaussian with variance \(1/D\) for large \(D\). The scaled intensity \(x=Du_i^2\) has the Porter–Thomas density \(P(x)=e^{-x/2}/\sqrt{2\pi x}\). Complex Haar vectors instead have exponentially distributed scaled intensities in the large-\(D\) limit. Orthogonality and normalization correlate components; treating them as independent Gaussians is an approximation justified only for suitable low-order questions at large dimension.
Let \(A\) be a fixed real symmetric observable and remove its identity part, \(A_c=A-(\operatorname{Tr}A/D)I\). Orthogonal invariance gives
\[
\mathbb E A_{nn}=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}A}{D},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(A_{nn})=
\frac{2\operatorname{Tr}A_c^2}{D(D+2)}.
\tag{3.7}\]
The typical off-diagonal variance is asymptotically half this value. For a bounded local observable, \(\operatorname{Tr}A_c^2\) is normally proportional to \(D\), so fluctuations scale as \(D^{-1/2}\) in amplitude. When \(D\) grows exponentially with system size, individual fluctuations are exponentially small. The trace part contributes equally to all diagonal elements and nothing off diagonal.
This calculation provides a seed for ETH, but a full random matrix loses the energy dependence of physical observables. It has no spatial geometry, propagation speed, transport law, or meaningful low-energy quasiparticles. A physical many-body observable typically has a frequency-dependent band profile in the energy basis, which the ETH ansatz restores.

title: 3  Random matrices and the fingerprints of quantum chaos
text:
3.5 From classical dynamics to wavefunctions
The Berry–Tabor proposal associates generic regular semiclassical systems with Poisson spectra, subject to nondegeneracy and genericity assumptions  [2]. The Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit proposal associates sufficiently chaotic semiclassical systems with the appropriate random-matrix correlations  [3]. Neither says that a harmonic oscillator is Poisson or that every chaotic spectrum is GOE: exact degeneracies, arithmetic structure, and antiunitary symmetries matter.
Berry’s random-wave picture provides a complementary eigenfunction hypothesis  [4]. For a free particle well inside a two-dimensional chaotic billiard, build a wavefunction from many plane waves of equal wave number \(k\) with random phases and isotropically distributed directions. A central-limit argument makes the local amplitude approximately Gaussian. Angular averaging gives the illustrative correlator
\[
\mathbb E[\psi^*(\mathbf r)\psi(\mathbf r')]
\simeq\frac1V\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\mathrm d\phi}{2\pi}
e^{ik\hat{\mathbf n}(\phi)\cdot(\mathbf r'-\mathbf r)}
=\frac1V J_0(k|\mathbf r'-\mathbf r|).
\tag{3.8}\]
The energy constraint fixes the wavelength even though the phases are random. Boundary conditions, short periodic orbits, scars, and mixed dynamics produce corrections. A random wave is therefore an energy-constrained statistical model, richer than a vector whose position-space entries are all unrelated.






NoteWhat the diagnostics establish



Agreement with a spacing distribution is numerical evidence for a universality class over the tested scales. It does not prove eigenstate thermalization for every observable, nor set a relaxation time. Eigenvectors, operator matrix elements, and dynamics must be examined separately.

3.6 Exercises and worked answers
1. Normalize the GOE surmise. Starting from \(P(s)=as e^{-bs^2}\), impose normalization and mean spacing one.






TipAnswer





\(\int_0^\infty s e^{-bs^2}\,\mathrm ds=1/(2b)\) gives \(a=2b\). The mean condition gives \(a\sqrt\pi/(4b^{3/2})=1\), hence \(b=\pi/4\) and \(a=\pi/2\).



2. Derive the Poisson ratio law. Take independent unit-mean exponential gaps \(x,y\).






TipAnswer





On the region \(x\le y\), use \(x=ry\), with Jacobian \(y\). The two equivalent regions give \(P(r)=2\int_0^\infty y e^{-(1+r)y}\,\mathrm dy=2/(1+r)^2\). Integrating \(rP(r)\) from zero to one yields \(2\ln2-1\).



3. An identity operator test. Why must the identity part be subtracted in Equation 3.7?






TipAnswer





For \(A=aI\), every basis gives \(A_{nn}=a\) and \(A_{mn}=0\) for \(m\ne n\). A formula using \(\operatorname{Tr}A^2\) alone would predict fluctuations that do not exist. Subtracting \(aI\) leaves \(A_c=0\), as required.

title: 4  Physical many-body Hamiltonians and eigenstate structure
text:
4.1 Two useful model families
Random matrices explain universal fluctuations, but a many-body Hamiltonian has much more structure than an invariant ensemble. This chapter connects the two descriptions through concrete lattice models, symmetry sectors, and energy-constrained eigenstates. The distinction matters because a state may be spread over many basis vectors without giving thermal predictions.
For spin-\(1/2\) degrees of freedom on an open chain, consider
\[
H_{\mathrm{Ising}}=J\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}\sigma_j^z\sigma_{j+1}^z
+h_x\sum_{j=1}^L\sigma_j^x+h_z\sum_{j=1}^L\sigma_j^z.
\tag{4.1}\]
Here \(\sigma^\alpha\) has eigenvalues \(\pm1\), and the Hilbert-space dimension is \(2^L\). The \(h_z=0\) transverse-field Ising chain is integrable: a transformation to fermions reduces it to independent quasiparticle modes. Generic nonzero transverse and longitudinal fields remove that free-particle solution. “Generic” excludes special limits and does not imply a theorem of ETH. With real couplings, complex conjugation is an antiunitary symmetry in the \(\sigma^z\) basis, so GOE is the relevant benchmark within a fully resolved real symmetry sector. This antiunitary operation need not coincide with physical reversal of every spin.
A particle-conserving example uses spinless fermions or hard-core bosons:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H={}&-t\sum_j(c_j^\dagger c_{j+1}+\text{h.c.})
+V\sum_j(n_j-\tfrac12)(n_{j+1}-\tfrac12)\\
&-t'\sum_j(c_j^\dagger c_{j+2}+\text{h.c.})
+V'\sum_j(n_j-\tfrac12)(n_{j+2}-\tfrac12).
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.2}\]
For the usual uniform one-dimensional chain the nearest-neighbor limit connects to the integrable XXZ model; next-nearest-neighbor terms generically break integrability. Fixing particle number \(N\) gives dimension \(\binom LN\), already exponential near half filling. Boundary conditions and particle statistics require care: fermionic hopping acquires occupation-dependent signs, and periodic hard-core bosons and fermions do not always share identical boundary sectors. Exact diagonalization studies such as  [1] use these families to examine the crossover between integrability and chaos.

title: 4  Physical many-body Hamiltonians and eigenstate structure
text:
4.2 Why symmetry reduction is physics
A symmetry \(Q\) satisfying \([H,Q]=0\) divides the Hilbert space into invariant subspaces. Diagonalization may be performed separately in each one. This both reduces computational cost and states which macroscopic information is being held fixed. Examples include total particle number, total magnetization, lattice momentum, and spatial reflection.
Two subtleties are common. First, noncommuting symmetry generators cannot in general all be fixed simultaneously. For example, reflection maps momentum \(k\) to \(-k\) and preserves an individual momentum sector only at special momenta. Second, if the preparation occupies several sectors, its sector weights are conserved. An equilibrium comparison must keep those weights or justify why the chosen observable cannot distinguish them.
In the Ising chain, the spin-flip operator \(\prod_j\sigma_j^x\) is a symmetry at \(h_z=0\) and is broken by a generic longitudinal field. Reflection remains for a spatially uniform open chain. A boundary perturbation can remove reflection, but one must then describe the perturbed Hamiltonian explicitly. Hidden unremoved symmetries can imitate integrable level statistics.

title: 4  Physical many-body Hamiltonians and eigenstate structure
section: 4.3 Eigenstates in a physically chosen basis
text:
4.3 Eigenstates in a physically chosen basis
Write \(H=H_0+\lambda V\), where \(H_0\ket\alpha=\epsilon_\alpha\ket\alpha\), and expand
\[
\ket n=\sum_\alpha C_\alpha^{(n)}\ket\alpha,\qquad
\sum_\alpha|C_\alpha^{(n)}|^2=1.
\tag{4.3}\]
The basis should answer a physical question: occupation states reveal configuration-space structure; an integrable \(H_0\) basis reveals hybridization between its eigenstates. No basis-independent notion of participation exists, because the energy basis makes every exact eigenstate occupy a single vector.
For weights \(w_\alpha=|C_\alpha^{(n)}|^2\), useful measures are the Shannon entropy and inverse participation ratio:
\[
S_{\mathrm{Sh}}=-\sum_\alpha w_\alpha\ln w_\alpha,\qquad
\mathrm{IPR}=\sum_\alpha w_\alpha^2,\qquad
\mathrm{PR}=\mathrm{IPR}^{-1}.
\tag{4.4}\]
A uniform superposition over \(M\) vectors gives \(S_{\mathrm{Sh}}=\ln M\) and \(\mathrm{PR}=M\). A real Haar vector has mean IPR \(3/(D+2)\), so a typical participation ratio is of order \(D/3\). This is a benchmark for random amplitudes, not a universal target: physical states often fill only the part of the basis consistent with their energy.
A basis state \(\ket\alpha\) has mean final-Hamiltonian energy \(E_\alpha=\bra\alpha H\ket\alpha\) and energy variance
\[
\sigma_\alpha^2=\bra\alpha H^2\ket\alpha-E_\alpha^2
=\sum_{\gamma\ne\alpha}|H_{\gamma\alpha}|^2.
\tag{4.5}\]
Only configurations connected by the Hamiltonian appear in this exact expression. Few-body interactions make the matrix sparse and constrain the accessible energy envelope. The energy-shell picture asks whether coefficients fluctuate randomly within that physically allowed envelope. It does not assume equal weight across the entire spectrum.  [2] uses this viewpoint to connect eigenstate structure with relaxation.
Perturbation theory offers a useful local criterion. For an unperturbed state \(\ket\alpha\), the leading amplitude on \(\ket\gamma\) is approximately \(\lambda V_{\gamma\alpha}/(\epsilon_\alpha-\epsilon_\gamma)\). A near resonance invalidates this expansion even if \(\lambda\) is small. Because many-body level spacings become very small with size, weak interactions can hybridize many states. Yet the relevant denominator is the spacing among states connected by the perturbation, together with its selection rules, rather than indiscriminately the smallest spacing in the entire Hilbert space. This distinction helps explain why local interactions, sparse connectivity, and conserved quantities leave structure absent from a full random matrix.
A smooth envelope and irregular internal coefficients play different roles. The envelope determines which energies and configurations are accessible; coefficient statistics describe fluctuations within that support. Increasing participation can initially reflect a widening envelope, before the internal coefficients resemble random variables. Comparing nearby eigenstates at the same energy and in the same physical basis helps separate these effects.

title: 4  Physical many-body Hamiltonians and eigenstate structure
section: 4.4 Local density of states and survival probability
text:
4.4 Local density of states and survival probability
The local density of states (LDOS), also called the strength function, of a preparation \(\ket{\psi_0}\) is
\[
F_{\psi_0}(E)=\sum_n|\braket{n}{\psi_0}|^2\delta(E-E_n).
\tag{4.6}\]
Its moments are the energy moments in the initial state. Its Fourier transform is the return amplitude,
\[
\mathcal G(t)=\bra{\psi_0}e^{-iHt/\hbar}\ket{\psi_0}
=\int\mathrm dE\,F_{\psi_0}(E)e^{-iEt/\hbar},\qquad
P_{\mathrm{surv}}(t)=|\mathcal G(t)|^2.
\tag{4.7}\]
An ideal Gaussian LDOS of variance \(\sigma_E^2\) gives \(P_{\mathrm{surv}}(t)=e^{-\sigma_E^2t^2/\hbar^2}\). An ideal Lorentzian of width \(\Gamma\) gives an exponential decay after Fourier transformation. A weak-coupling golden-rule regime can produce an approximately Lorentzian central profile, while stronger mixing may produce a roughly Gaussian envelope. Actual bounded spectra have edges and discrete levels, so neither ideal profile holds at all times.
A direct expansion, independent of either approximation, gives
\[
P_{\mathrm{surv}}(t)=1-\frac{\sigma_E^2t^2}{\hbar^2}+O(t^4)
\tag{4.8}\]
for a finite system. The early quadratic law shows why a purely exponential survival probability cannot start at \(t=0\). It also shows that fast decay of a return probability is controlled by energy spread, which alone does not establish thermalization of a local observable.

title: 4  Physical many-body Hamiltonians and eigenstate structure
text:
4.5 Entanglement adds a different diagnostic
Divide the chain into regions \(A\) and \(B\). The Schmidt decomposition is \(\ket\psi=\sum_{a=1}^\chi\sqrt{\lambda_a}\ket a_A\ket a_B\), where \(\lambda_a\ge0\) and \(\sum_a\lambda_a=1\). Both reduced states share the nonzero eigenvalues \(\lambda_a\), and
\[
S_A=-\sum_a\lambda_a\ln\lambda_a=S_B,
\qquad S_A\le\ln\min(d_A,d_B).
\tag{4.9}\]
Highly excited thermal eigenstates of many local chaotic systems have entropy proportional to subsystem volume when \(A\) is small compared with the whole system. At finite energy density the coefficient is the thermodynamic entropy density, under subsystem ETH assumptions. Ground states, localized eigenstates, and constrained subspaces can behave differently.
For a Haar-random complex pure state in an unconstrained product space with \(d_A\le d_B\), the Page average is
\[
\mathbb E S_A=\sum_{k=d_B+1}^{d_Ad_B}\frac1k-
\frac{d_A-1}{2d_B}
\simeq\ln d_A-\frac{d_A}{2d_B},
\tag{4.10}\]
where the final expression assumes large dimensions. The exact expression was proposed by  [3] and proved in subsequent work, including  [4]. The unrestricted Haar average is a useful high-temperature benchmark. Fixed energy, particle number, or other constraints change the appropriate random-state ensemble and its finite-size corrections. Agreement with an unrestricted Page estimate is not required at a general temperature.
Participation entropy and entanglement entropy ask different questions. A product of local equal superpositions occupies every computational basis vector but has no entanglement. Conversely, a state can have large bipartite entropy while preserving special correlations that make some observables nonthermal. No single scalar diagnoses all aspects of chaos.

title: 4  Physical many-body Hamiltonians and eigenstate structure
text:
4.6 Exercises and worked answers
1. Derive the shell width. Starting from \(\bra\alpha H^2\ket\alpha\), establish Equation 4.5.






TipAnswer





Insert \(I=\sum_\gamma\ket\gamma\bra\gamma\) between the two Hamiltonians. Hermiticity gives \(\bra\alpha H^2\ket\alpha=\sum_\gamma|H_{\gamma\alpha}|^2\). The diagonal term is \(E_\alpha^2\), which cancels in the variance.



2. Delocalized but unentangled. Evaluate the computational-basis participation and bipartite entropy of \(\ket+^{\otimes L}\), where \(\ket+=(\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\).






TipAnswer





Every configuration has weight \(2^{-L}\), so \(\mathrm{PR}=2^L\) and \(S_{\mathrm{Sh}}=L\ln2\). The state factorizes across every spatial cut, giving \(S_A=0\). Computational-basis delocalization alone does not imply entanglement or thermal behavior.



3. Return plateau. Assuming nondegenerate energies, find the infinite-time average of \(P_{\mathrm{surv}}(t)\).






TipAnswer





Writing \(p_n=|\braket n{\psi_0}|^2\) gives \(P_{\mathrm{surv}}(t)=\sum_{mn}p_mp_ne^{i(E_m-E_n)t/\hbar}\). Time averaging removes terms with \(m\ne n\), leaving \(\sum_np_n^2\). Its inverse is the effective number of populated energy eigenstates. Energy degeneracies require combining weights within equal-energy subspaces.

[2] L. F. Santos, F. Borgonovi, and F. M. Izrailev, Chaos and statistical relaxation in quantum systems of interacting particles, Physical Review Letters 108, 094102 (2012).


[3] D. N. Page, Average entropy of a subsystem, Physical Review Letters 71, 1291 (1993).


[4] S. Sen, Average entropy of a quantum subsystem, Physical Review Letters 77, 1 (1996).

title: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration
text:
5.1 Exact unitary dynamics and the diagonal ensemble
The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis makes a striking claim: for suitable observables, an individual energy eigenstate already carries the equilibrium equation of state. Time evolution is then needed to suppress observable coherences, while the equilibrium value is encoded in the eigenstates themselves. We first establish what dephasing proves exactly, and then identify the additional hypothesis that makes equilibrium thermal.
Let \(H\ket n=E_n\ket n\) and expand a pure initial state as \(\ket{\psi_0}=\sum_nc_n\ket n\). For a Hermitian observable \(A\), write \(A_{mn}=\bra m A\ket n\) and \(p_n=|c_n|^2\). Its expectation is
\[
A(t)=\sum_np_nA_{nn}
+\sum_{m\ne n}c_m^*c_n e^{i(E_m-E_n)t/\hbar}A_{mn}.
\tag{5.1}\]
Define the infinite-time average \(\overline{X}=\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\tau^{-1}\int_0^\tau X(t)\,\mathrm dt\). Since the time average of \(e^{i\omega t}\) vanishes for nonzero \(\omega\), nondegenerate energies imply
\[
\overline{A(t)}=A_{\mathrm{DE}}=\sum_np_nA_{nn},\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{DE}}=\sum_np_n\ket n\bra n.
\tag{5.2}\]
If energies are degenerate, the exact averaged density matrix is instead \(\overline\rho=\sum_E P_E\rho_0P_E\): coherences within an equal-energy subspace remain. The diagonal ensemble is thus shorthand for dephasing in the appropriate energy blocks, not a physical stochastic projection during closed-system evolution.
The diagonal weights retain memory of the preparation. There is no general reason for \(\rho_{\mathrm{DE}}\) to equal a Gibbs state. Furthermore, an average alone does not say that the signal stays near its average. A pendulum also has a time average while continuing to oscillate with finite amplitude.
crumbs: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration

title: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration
text:
5.2 A rigorous variance bound
Assume nonresonant nonzero gaps: \(E_m-E_n=E_p-E_q\) with \(m\ne n\) implies \((m,n)=(p,q)\). Squaring the fluctuating term in Equation 5.1 and averaging gives the exact identity
\[
\overline{|A(t)-A_{\mathrm{DE}}|^2}
=\sum_{m\ne n}p_mp_n|A_{mn}|^2.
\tag{5.3}\]
Define the effective dimension \(d_{\mathrm{eff}}=(\sum_np_n^2)^{-1}\). Using \(p_mp_n\le(p_m^2+p_n^2)/2\), Hermiticity, and \(\sum_n|A_{mn}|^2=\bra m A^2\ket m\le\|A\|^2\) yields
\[
\overline{|A(t)-A_{\mathrm{DE}}|^2}
\le\|A\|^2\sum_np_n^2
=\frac{\|A\|^2}{d_{\mathrm{eff}}}.
\tag{5.4}\]
Here \(\|A\|\) is the operator norm. Subtracting a constant multiple of the identity may tighten the bound without changing the fluctuations. Chebyshev’s inequality then bounds the long-time fraction of instants with \(|A(t)-A_{\mathrm{DE}}|>\epsilon\) by \(\|A\|^2/(d_{\mathrm{eff}}\epsilon^2)\). Degenerate gaps can be accommodated by multiplying suitable bounds by their maximal degeneracy, rather than silently using Equation 5.3.
This result establishes equilibration for many populated levels and a bounded observable under its spectral assumptions. It is not a proof of a Gibbs value, monotonic relaxation, or a practical equilibration time. It is also not necessary: an energy eigenstate has \(d_{\mathrm{eff}}=1\) but is exactly stationary. Rigorous work by  [1] and  [2] develops broad equilibration results with carefully stated preparation, spectral, and subsystem assumptions.

title: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration
text:
5.3 The ETH ansatz
For a local or few-body observable in a chaotic many-body system, the standard form is
\[
A_{mn}=\mathcal A(\bar E)\delta_{mn}
+e^{-S(\bar E)/2}f_A(\bar E,\omega)R_{mn},
\qquad
\bar E=\frac{E_m+E_n}{2},\qquad
\omega=\frac{E_m-E_n}{\hbar}.
\tag{5.5}\]
\(\mathcal A(E)\) is a smooth equilibrium function; \(S(E)\) is a thermodynamic entropy associated with the density of states in a fixed reference energy interval; \(f_A\) is a smooth frequency envelope; and \(R_{mn}\) describes irregular order-one fluctuations after averaging within small energy-frequency bins. The diagonal variance can differ from the off-diagonal variance by a symmetry-dependent factor. Hermiticity requires compatible conjugation properties, for example \(f_A(\bar E,-\omega)=f_A(\bar E,\omega)^*\) in a convention where \(R_{nm}=R_{mn}^*\).
The reference interval makes \(e^{S}\) dimensionless; a change of convention is absorbed into \(f_A\). The actual matrix elements of a fixed Hamiltonian are deterministic. The ansatz models their local statistical behavior and does not assert that all \(R_{mn}\) are independent. Exact identities, conservation laws, and higher correlation functions constrain them. The early proposals of  [3] and  [4], followed by the matrix-element formulation in  [5], provide the conceptual basis of ETH.
Why the exponential? The number of states in a many-body shell is \(D\sim e^S\). Random-orientation estimates in Chapter 3 make individual matrix-element fluctuations of a bounded local observable scale as \(D^{-1/2}\). Conversely, the spectral sum \(\sum_m|A_{mn}|^2=\bra n A^2\ket n\) remains finite because approximately \(e^S\) small contributions add. Physical locality and dynamics determine the envelope \(f_A\); a full invariant random matrix cannot provide that frequency structure.

title: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration
section: 5.4 How diagonal ETH produces thermal values
text:
5.4 How diagonal ETH produces thermal values
Suppose the preparation has mean energy \(E_0=\sum_np_nE_n\) and variance \(\sigma_E^2=\sum_np_n(E_n-E_0)^2\). Diagonal ETH gives
\[
A_{\mathrm{DE}}=\sum_np_n\mathcal A(E_n)
+\sum_np_n\delta A_n
=\mathcal A(E_0)+\frac12\mathcal A''(E_0)\sigma_E^2+\cdots
+\sum_np_n\delta A_n.
\tag{5.6}\]
The linear term vanishes by definition of \(E_0\). For an intensive local observable, write \(\mathcal A(E)=a(E/L)\). Then \(\mathcal A''(E)=a''(e)/L^2\). If \(\sigma_E^2=O(L)\), the curvature correction is \(O(1/L)\) where \(a\) is smooth. If eigenstate deviations are uniformly small in the occupied window, their weighted sum is also small regardless of the detailed weights \(p_n\).
The microcanonical average over a narrow window tends to the same \(\mathcal A(E_0)\). Under ensemble equivalence, a canonical state with matching mean energy also gives it. Thus the mechanism has three distinct ingredients: narrow energy density, smooth and thermal diagonal matrix elements, and sufficiently small observable coherences for most times. The diagonal density matrices themselves need never coincide.
Off-diagonal ETH also estimates temporal fluctuations. Near a fixed energy density, \(|A_{mn}|^2\sim e^{-S}|f_A|^2\) makes Equation 5.3 small. Nevertheless, correlations between initial amplitudes and matrix elements, low-frequency hydrodynamic structure, and conserved quantities affect the approach to equilibrium. The entropy factor alone does not determine a relaxation rate.

title: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration
section: 5.5 Weak ETH, strong ETH, and observable choice
text:
5.5 Weak ETH, strong ETH, and observable choice
Fix a sequence of energy-density windows and an observable. Weak ETH says that the fraction of eigenstates whose expectation differs appreciably from the thermal value goes to zero with increasing size. Strong ETH requires the maximum deviation in that window to vanish. Numerical standard deviations probe typical fluctuations; testing the largest outliers is a different task.
Weak ETH does not thermalize every preparation: a state can place appreciable weight on a vanishing fraction of exceptional eigenstates. Strong diagonal ETH removes that particular obstruction for narrow-energy preparations, but dephasing and the observation time still matter. Neither form is intended to apply to all operators. The projector onto a chosen eigenstate is deliberately constructed to distinguish that state, and a conserved operator has special matrix structure. The physically relevant class is typically local, few-body, or otherwise restricted by the measurement protocol.

title: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration
section: 5.6 The quantum ergodic theorem and its limits
text:
5.6 The quantum ergodic theorem and its limits
One can describe macroscopic observations using a coarse decomposition \(\mathcal H_R= igoplus_
u\mathcal H_
u\) with projectors \(P_
u\) and dimensions \(d_
u\). Equilibrium weights are \(d_
u/D_R\). Von Neumann’s quantum ergodic theorem, with nonresonance and suitable large macrospaces, establishes normal behavior for typical relative orientations of these macrospaces and the Hamiltonian eigenbasis: every initial vector has macrospace weights close to equilibrium for most times  [6].
The quantifiers are essential. This is a rigorous typicality statement about macroscopic decompositions, not a proof that every specified local Hamiltonian has thermal eigenstates. It does not supply an experimentally useful time scale or make the fine-grained entropy increase. ETH instead asks whether physically given observables have the required structure in a physically given Hamiltonian.
Integrable systems, localized systems, special nonthermal eigenstates, phase coexistence, and approximate conservation laws delimit ETH’s use. They are not reasons to discard equilibration: a system can equilibrate to a constrained or preparation-dependent value. Later chapters examine these alternatives.

title: 5  Eigenstate thermalization and quantum equilibration
text:
5.7 Exercises and worked answers
1. A nonthermal stationary state. Does stationarity imply thermalization?






TipAnswer





No. Any energy eigenstate is stationary. In a Hamiltonian that violates diagonal ETH, a local expectation in an eigenstate can differ from the microcanonical result at the same energy. Stationarity establishes neither the thermal value nor initial-state independence.



2. Two-level coherence. For \(c_1=c_2=1/\sqrt2\), derive the temporal variance when the gap is nonzero.






TipAnswer





The oscillation is \(\operatorname{Re}[A_{12}e^{i(E_1-E_2)t/\hbar}]\) after absorbing the relative initial phase. Its time-averaged square is \(|A_{12}|^2/2\). This agrees with Equation 5.3, which includes the ordered pairs \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\), each weighted by \(1/4\).



3. A curvature error. If \(a(e)=a_0+a_1e+a_2e^2\) and \(\sigma_E^2=cL\), what is the leading diagonal-ensemble shift from \(a(E_0/L)\) when diagonal ETH is exact?






TipAnswer





The shift is exactly \(a_2\sigma_E^2/L^2=a_2c/L\). Finite energy width gives a correction even when every eigenstate obeys the smooth ETH function. This correction should not be mistaken for an ETH violation.

title: 6  Quantum quenches and numerical tests of thermalization
text:
6.1 What a quench fixes
A quantum quench prepares an out-of-equilibrium state without maintaining contact with a reservoir. One prepares a state using an initial Hamiltonian \(H_i\), changes a parameter rapidly, and evolves with a final Hamiltonian \(H_f\). The state is continuous across an ideal sudden quench; the Hamiltonian and its energy eigenbasis change. This clean separation makes quenches a direct test of the mechanism developed in Chapter 5.
Suppose \(\ket{\psi_0}\) is an eigenstate, ground state, or experimentally prepared state associated with \(H_i\). Immediately after the change,
\[
E_0=\bra{\psi_0}H_f\ket{\psi_0},\qquad
\sigma_E^2=\bra{\psi_0}H_f^2\ket{\psi_0}-E_0^2,
\qquad p_n=|\braket{n_f}{\psi_0}|^2.
\tag{6.1}\]
Energy need not be conserved during the switch because an external agent changes the Hamiltonian. After the switch, the entire final-energy distribution \(p_n\) is constant. Unitary evolution changes relative phases. A finite switching time is a different protocol and must be modeled if it is not short compared with the relevant dynamical time scales.
For a local Hamiltonian \(H_f=\sum_jh_j\) and a product state or a state with rapidly decaying connected correlations,
\[
\sigma_E^2=\sum_{jk}\bigl(\langle h_jh_k\rangle
-\langle h_j\rangle\langle h_k\rangle\bigr)=O(L).
\tag{6.2}\]
The argument is that each \(j\) has only a bounded sum of appreciable connected correlations with other sites. It can fail for states with sufficiently long-range correlations. When it holds, the width in energy density vanishes even though exponentially many eigenstates can be occupied. This is the natural quench setting for diagonal ETH.

title: 6  Quantum quenches and numerical tests of thermalization
text:
6.2 Three stationary predictions
For the final Hamiltonian, the diagonal prediction is
\[
A_{\mathrm{DE}}=\sum_np_nA_{nn}.
\tag{6.3}\]
It retains the preparation and is exact as an infinite-time average when energies are nondegenerate. A microcanonical comparison uses
\[
A_{\mathrm{MC}}=\frac1{D_\Delta}
\sum_{|E_n-E_0|<\Delta}A_{nn},\qquad
D_\Delta=\#\{n:|E_n-E_0|<\Delta\}.
\tag{6.4}\]
The symbol \(\Delta\) here denotes the half-width of the chosen window. A canonical prediction is
\[
A_{\mathrm{CE}}=\frac{\sum_ne^{-\beta E_n}A_{nn}}{\sum_ne^{-\beta E_n}},
\qquad
\frac{\sum_nE_ne^{-\beta E_n}}{\sum_ne^{-\beta E_n}}=E_0.
\tag{6.5}\]
The last equation defines the comparison temperature, rather than assuming the initial Hamiltonian’s temperature survives the quench. For bounded spectra, energies above the infinite-temperature mean can require negative \(\beta\). This is mathematically consistent because the partition sum remains finite. The existence of such states does not imply that all unbounded physical systems admit negative absolute temperature.
All three predictions must enforce the same exact charges. If the state has several symmetry-sector weights, use weighted sector ensembles or establish equivalence for the observables being compared. A canonical average over an unconstrained Hilbert space can fail for the elementary reason that it permits an incorrect particle number.
Even in a chaotic system, DE, MC, and CE are not identical at finite size. They sample different energy distributions. The curvature term in Equation 5.6 predicts part of this difference. Near a critical region, a spectral edge, or a small window containing only a few levels, finite-size differences can be substantial.

section: 6.3 What to measure in an exact-diagonalization study
text:
6.3 What to measure in an exact-diagonalization study
A transparent test begins with the complete Hamiltonian, boundary conditions, local-operator convention, and symmetry sector. Plot \(A_{nn}\) against energy density, and show the window occupied by the initial state. A smooth curve with decreasing scatter as size grows supports diagonal ETH. A single small-system plot is an illustration, not a thermodynamic-limit result.
Useful measurements include a root-mean-square deviation within a window, the largest deviation, neighboring-eigenstate differences, and binned off-diagonal variances as functions of mean energy and frequency. These answer different questions. The window must be narrow enough to remove smooth energy dependence and wide enough to contain many states. Subtracting a local smooth fit can help measure fluctuations, but the fitting procedure must be reported because overfitting can artificially suppress them.
For a quench, evaluate \(A(t)\) and compare its late-time average with \(A_{\mathrm{DE}}\) before using a thermal ensemble. Failure of the first comparison can reveal a time window too short for dephasing, numerical errors, or unresolved degeneracy. Agreement of DE with MC tests the thermal eigenstate mechanism for the occupied states. Agreement of MC with CE tests ensemble equivalence for the observable and system size.
The numerical work of  [1] provided a direct lattice-system test connecting eigenstate expectation values to quench outcomes. Studies across integrability breaking, including  [2], also show why spectral and eigenvector diagnostics should be examined together. These are results for specified model families and finite-size sequences, not blanket proofs for arbitrary interacting Hamiltonians.

title: 6  Quantum quenches and numerical tests of thermalization
text:
6.4 A reproducible small-chain illustration
The numerical laboratory implements an open chain with \(L=9\) and
\[
H=-\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}Z_jZ_{j+1}
-1.05\sum_{j=1}^LX_j
-\sum_{j=1}^L(0.35+0.07j)Z_j.
\tag{6.6}\]
Here \(X_j,Z_j\) are Pauli matrices, and \(\hbar=1\). The varying longitudinal field removes reflection symmetry and provides a concrete interacting real Hamiltonian. The observable is the central spin \(Z_5\). Among computational-basis product states with central spin \(+1\), the script chooses the one whose mean energy is nearest the spectral mean. Its subsequent motion is an exact unitary calculation for this finite chain.






Figure 6.1: A small-chain illustration of eigenstate expectation values and quench dynamics. The Hamiltonian is Equation 6.6; the observable is the central Pauli Z. The horizontal comparisons are the exact diagonal ensemble and a microcanonical window with half-width 0.8 in the displayed energy units. The numerical laboratory gives the preparation rule, code, and verification.



Read this figure as a demonstration of the computation and of finite-size questions. To infer ETH scaling, repeat for several larger sizes with consistent energy-density windows and observables. To infer a relaxation law, specify the fitting interval and test its stability. No large-system conclusion follows from visually smooth behavior at \(L=9\).

title: 6  Quantum quenches and numerical tests of thermalization
section: 6.5 Recurrences, times, and the order of limits
text:
6.5 Recurrences, times, and the order of limits
A finite isolated spectrum produces a quasiperiodic sum of phases. Arbitrarily close recurrences are possible; exact irreversible convergence of the full state cannot occur. Equilibration therefore means closeness of selected observables for most times, often after an initial transient, rather than convergence of every amplitude.
A finite-time average contains the exact kernel
\[
\frac1\tau\int_0^\tau e^{i\omega t}\,\mathrm dt
=e^{i\omega\tau/2}\frac{\sin(\omega\tau/2)}{\omega\tau/2}.
\tag{6.7}\]
Very small gaps have not dephased when \(\tau\ll1/|\omega|\). However, an observable may equilibrate much earlier than the inverse smallest many-body gap because its relevant matrix elements and preparation weights need not resolve that extreme gap. Local transport, quasiparticle lifetimes, and approximate charges can dominate the experimentally relevant time.
The limits \(L\to\infty\) and \(t\to\infty\) can lead to different questions. Taking the infinite-time average at fixed finite \(L\) gives DE. Taking a thermodynamic limit first can support smooth relaxation laws and continuous spectra. A finite numerical study should state which quantity it estimates and avoid treating its recurrence time as a material relaxation time.

title: 6  Quantum quenches and numerical tests of thermalization
text:
6.6 Why integrable quenches differ
At integrability, additional charges constrain \(p_n\) beyond energy. Nearby eigenstates can have different local properties even when their energy densities agree. The diagonal ensemble can then relax to a value different from MC or CE. A generalized Gibbs ensemble is designed to keep the additional locally relevant constraints; later chapters construct it explicitly.
Several caveats remain. Some observables in integrable models can still show thermal-looking values for particular preparations. A large effective dimension can make temporal fluctuations small even when the stationary value is nonthermal. Conversely, an approximately conserved quantity in a weakly nonintegrable model can produce a long prethermal plateau before eventual drift. The criterion for thermalization is a comparison of stationary local predictions under specified constraints, not whether a curve becomes visually flat.

title: 6  Quantum quenches and numerical tests of thermalization
text:
6.7 Exercises and worked answers
1. Exact energy width in the lab preparation. For any \(Z\)-product state in Equation 6.6, find \(\sigma_E^2\).






TipAnswer





The \(ZZ\) and \(Z\) terms are diagonal in the preparation. Each transverse term flips a distinct spin, producing an orthogonal configuration with amplitude \(-1.05\). By Equation 4.5, \(\sigma_E^2=L(1.05)^2\). The mean energy depends on the chosen spin configuration, but this variance does not.



2. Solving for temperature. Why is the canonical mean energy a monotone function of \(\beta\), and when is the solution unique?






TipAnswer





\(\partial_\beta\langle H\rangle_\beta=-\operatorname{Var}_\beta(H)\le0\). If more than one energy has nonzero thermal weight, the variance is positive and the function is strictly decreasing. For a finite nontrivial spectrum, any energy strictly between the lowest and highest levels has a unique finite \(\beta\) in the unrestricted sector; endpoints require limiting temperatures.



3. A finite-window bias. Why need the mean energy of a symmetric microcanonical window around \(E_0\) not equal \(E_0\)?






TipAnswer





The density of states need not be symmetric. More levels may lie on one side of the center, shifting the equally weighted mean. This matters when comparing energy-dependent observables at finite width. Report both the chosen window and its actual mean energy, or reduce the width while retaining enough levels.

title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
text:
7.1 From amplitudes to populations
An isolated quantum state evolves reversibly. Thermodynamics nevertheless describes directed changes: a stirred fluid warms, an uncontrolled distribution spreads, and a cyclic engine cannot extract work from an equilibrium reservoir. The connection requires us to specify both the preparation and the information retained. This chapter first proves several finite-dimensional statements that require no chaos. It then identifies the additional assumptions needed to interpret them thermodynamically. We set Boltzmann’s constant to one, so entropy is dimensionless and temperature has energy units.
Let a protocol change a Hamiltonian from \(H_i\) to \(H_f\), with eigenvectors \(\ket{n,i}\) and \(\ket{m,f}\). Its propagator \(U\) obeys \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\). Suppose the initial density matrix is diagonal in the initial energy basis:
\[
\rho_i=\sum_n p_n\ket{n,i}\bra{n,i}.
\]
The final energy populations are
\[
q_m=\sum_n T_{mn}p_n,
\qquad T_{mn}=\abs{\bra{m,f}U\ket{n,i}}^2.
\tag{7.1}\]
Normalization of each column of \(U\) gives \(\sum_mT_{mn}=1\), while completeness of its rows gives \(\sum_nT_{mn}=1\). Thus \(T\) is doubly stochastic: every entry is nonnegative and both its row and column sums equal one. A matrix constructed this way is called unistochastic. Every unistochastic matrix is doubly stochastic; the converse fails in dimensions above two.
The assumption about the initial state matters. For a coherent preparation,
\[
q_m=\sum_{n\ell}U_{mn}\rho_{n\ell}U_{m\ell}^*,
\]
and interference terms cannot generally be written as a fixed stochastic map acting on \(p_n=\rho_{nn}\). For example, a Hadamard rotation transforms \((\ket{0}+\ket{1})/\sqrt2\) into \(\ket{0}\). The populations change from \((1/2,1/2)\) to \((1,0)\) and their Shannon entropy decreases. Nothing violates unitary dynamics: the initial phase supplied the missing information.
A more general quantum channel \(\Phi\) is unital if \(\Phi(I)=I\). For a channel that also preserves trace, the matrix
\[
T_{mn}=\bra{m}\Phi(\ket{n}\bra{n})\ket{m}
\]
is doubly stochastic between any two orthonormal bases. Dephasing, random-unitary noise, and isolated unitary evolution are examples. Thermal amplitude damping is not unital; its preferred stationary state is generally Gibbs rather than uniform.

title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
text:
7.2 What a master equation assumes
A continuous population description takes the form
\[
\dot p_n=\sum_{m\ne n}\left[w_{nm}p_m-w_{mn}p_n\right]
=\sum_mL_{nm}p_m.
\tag{7.2}\]
Here \(w_{nm}\) is the rate from \(m\) to \(n\), \(L_{nm}=w_{nm}\) for \(n\ne m\), and \(L_{mm}=-\sum_{n\ne m}w_{nm}\). Column sums of \(L\) vanish automatically. The evolution \(e^{Lt}\) is also doubly stochastic precisely when its row sums vanish:
\[
\sum_{m\ne n}w_{nm}=\sum_{m\ne n}w_{mn}.
\]
Symmetric rates \(w_{nm}=w_{mn}\) are sufficient but stronger than necessary. One can have balanced circulation around a three-state ring without pairwise symmetry.
An exact isolated finite system does not automatically obey this equation. A Markov description discards memory and phase information. It may follow from weak perturbations, a separation between correlation and heating times, dephasing between kicks, or an explicit measurement protocol. Repeated coherent applications of \(U\) give \(U^r\), whereas repeated population maps give \(T^r\); these are different experiments. Before using a master equation, identify the physical mechanism making the discarded phases irrelevant.

title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
section: 7.3 Uniform populations: fixed point versus attractor
text:
7.3 Uniform populations: fixed point versus attractor
For \(D\) accessible levels, the vector \(u_n=1/D\) satisfies \(Tu=u\). This is the infinite-temperature state in that finite Hilbert space, or within the conserved symmetry sector being considered. Being stationary does not make it an attractor.
For a fixed matrix \(T\), convergence \(T^rp\to u\) for all \(p\) follows if \(T\) is primitive: some positive integer power has strictly positive entries. In a finite Markov chain this is equivalent to irreducibility together with aperiodicity. Irreducibility prevents isolated communicating blocks; aperiodicity prevents persistent cycles. The swap matrix
\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
preserves the uniform state but alternates every nonuniform distribution forever. An identity matrix preserves every distribution. Symmetry blocks similarly retain their initial total probabilities, even if each block mixes internally. A connected continuous-time chain with finite rates avoids the discrete-time periodicity obstruction. The constructive contraction proof is in Section 13.3.
There is also a physical limit to the phrase infinite-temperature attractor. An unbounded spectrum has no normalizable uniform distribution. A particle repeatedly accelerated by a vibrating wall can heat forever. In periodically driven many-body systems, approximate conservation and long prethermal intervals can delay heating; integrability, localization, or exact conserved quantities can obstruct the assumed mixing. The finite-matrix theorem applies only after its hypotheses are checked.

title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
section: 7.4 Three entropies and a rigorous inequality
text:
7.4 Three entropies and a rigorous inequality
The von Neumann entropy and the energy-basis diagonal entropy are
\[
S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho)=-\tr(\rho\ln\rho),\qquad
S_d(\rho;H)=-\sum_np_n\ln p_n,
\quad p_n=\bra n\rho\ket n.
\tag{7.3}\]
The latter is the Shannon entropy of energy measurement outcomes. It depends on the chosen basis; at degeneracies one must specify whether individual states or degenerate energy subspaces are resolved. A unitary preserves \(S_{\mathrm{vN}}\) exactly. Dephasing increases entropy, so \(S_d\ge S_{\mathrm{vN}}\); equality holds when \(\rho\) is already diagonal in the specified basis. Diagonal entropy was developed as a useful thermodynamic quantity for isolated driven systems by  [1].
For the initial diagonal preparations of Equation 7.1, concavity of \(f(x)=-x\ln x\) gives an elementary proof:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_d(q)&=\sum_m f\left(\sum_nT_{mn}p_n\right)\\
&\ge\sum_{mn}T_{mn}f(p_n)
=\sum_n f(p_n)=S_d(p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.4}\]
The row sums allow Jensen’s inequality; the column sums give the last equality. For an isolated protocol, this compares the endpoint populations when the initial state is diagonal. It does not establish that the instantaneous diagonal entropy is monotone at every time: coherence generated during the protocol can later be converted back into populations. Under genuinely Markovian doubly stochastic population evolution, the inequality applies to each time step and hence gives monotonicity.
A second proof uses relative entropy to the uniform vector:
\[
D(p\Vert u)=\sum_np_n\ln(p_n/u_n)=\ln D-S_d(p).
\]
Stochastic maps contract relative entropy and preserve \(u\), so \(D(Tp\Vert u)\le D(p\Vert u)\). This formulation extends naturally to Markov processes whose stationary distribution is nonuniform, although in that case Shannon entropy itself need not increase.

title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
text:
7.5 Kelvin’s principle from passivity
Order the levels as \(E_1\le\cdots\le E_D\). A diagonal state is passive when \(p_1\ge\cdots\ge p_D\). Consider a cyclic protocol, so the final Hamiltonian equals the initial one. Define work delivered to the system by
\[
W=\sum_nE_n(q_n-p_n).
\]
Let \(P_k=\sum_{n\le k}p_n\) and \(Q_k=\sum_{n\le k}q_n\). For a doubly stochastic map,
\[
Q_k=\sum_m a_mp_m,\quad
0\le a_m\le1,\quad\sum_ma_m=k.
\]
Among all such coefficients the largest sum assigns unit weight to the \(k\) largest \(p_m\). Therefore \(Q_k\le P_k\). Summation by parts then yields
\[
W=\sum_{k=1}^{D-1}(E_{k+1}-E_k)(P_k-Q_k)\ge0.
\tag{7.5}\]
Thus a cyclic operation cannot extract average work from a passive preparation. The conclusion needs neither ETH nor a large system. A positive-temperature Gibbs state is passive. A population-inverted state is not: swapping a more populated upper level with a less populated lower level extracts work. The stronger requirement that every number of independently prepared copies remain passive singles out equilibrium states under standard conditions; the mathematical theory is due to  [2].






NoteSolved example: a mixed two-level rotation



Take levels \(0,\epsilon\) and probabilities \((p,1-p)\) with \(p\ge1/2\). A rotation with transition probability \(r=\sin^2\theta\) has
\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}1-r&r\\r&1-r\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The upper-level population becomes \(1-p+r(2p-1)\), so \(W=\epsilon r(2p-1)\ge0\). The deviation from uniformity is multiplied by \(1-2r\). Repetition converges for \(0<r<1\), except at \(r=1\), when the two populations simply swap. Entropy increases even when a step carries the distribution through the uniform point to its opposite side.
