title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
section: 7.6 When diagonal entropy becomes thermodynamic entropy
text:
7.6 When diagonal entropy becomes thermodynamic entropy
A thermodynamic entropy \(S(E,\lambda)\) counts available states near energy \(E\). Write the density of states as \(\Omega(E,\lambda)\) and use a specified small energy width \(\delta E\) to define \(S=\ln[\Omega\delta E]\). In a macroscopic short-range system, different reasonable shell widths change only subextensive terms.
A narrow energy distribution is necessary for a single temperature but is not sufficient to make \(S_d\) equal \(S(E,\lambda)\). A single eigenstate has \(S_d=0\), even when ETH gives thermal local observables and \(S(E,\lambda)\) is extensive. Thermodynamic entropy counts compatible states; diagonal entropy records probabilities of the actual energy measurement preparation. Do not identify them for every state.
A useful sufficient condition is a nonsparse, smooth population distribution occupying exponentially many levels in a narrow shell, with no extensive information beyond energy. Partition the spectrum into bins \(a\) with \(g_a\) states and probabilities \(q_a\). If populations are nearly uniform inside each bin,
\[
S_d=-\sum_aq_a\ln q_a+\sum_aq_a\ln g_a.
\]
When the distribution has width \(\sigma_E=o(N)\), the first term is subextensive, the entropy density is smooth across the occupied region, and within-bin nonuniformity has subextensive relative entropy, this becomes \(S_d=S(\bar E,\lambda)+o(N)\). Chaos supports equilibration of simple observables and often the required smooth population statistics after ordinary preparations; it does not logically force this condition for arbitrarily engineered states. Numerical examples of diagonal entropy after quenches are studied in  [3].

title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
text:
7.7 Fundamental relation and first law
Define the equilibrium generalized force and temperature by
\[
F=-\ev{\partial_\lambda H}_{\mathrm{eq}},\qquad
\beta=\frac1T=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial E}\right)_\lambda.
\]
For a Gibbs distribution \(p_n=e^{-\beta E_n}/Z\), normalization gives
\[
\dd S=-\sum_n\dd p_n\ln p_n
=\beta\sum_nE_n\dd p_n.
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
\dd E=\sum_nE_n\dd p_n+\sum_np_n\dd E_n.
\]
Hellmann–Feynman gives \(\dd E_n=\bra n\partial_\lambda H\ket n\dd\lambda\); hence
\[
\dd E=T\dd S-F\dd\lambda.
\tag{7.6}\]
This is a differential identity on the equilibrium state manifold. Through ensemble equivalence and ETH, the force can also be measured in a suitable narrow-energy chaotic state. Finite systems can require corrections: surface and enclosed-volume microcanonical entropies need not give identical derivatives. For the volume \(\mathcal V(E,\lambda)=\tr\Theta(E-H)\), direct differentiation gives \(\partial_\lambda\mathcal V=\Omega F_{\mathrm{mc}}\) and \(\partial_E\mathcal V=\Omega\), making the analogous volume-entropy identity exact when its derivatives are well defined.
The first law instead expresses energy bookkeeping along an actual process:
\[
\dd E=\delta Q+\delta W_{\mathrm{on}}.
\]
For an externally driven isolated quantum system, exact unitary dynamics gives \(\dot E=\ev{\partial_\lambda H}\dot\lambda\) and \(\delta Q=0\). It may produce diagonal entropy while doing dissipative work. Only for a reversible quasistatic equilibrium path can one identify \(\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}=T\dd S\) and \(\delta W_{\mathrm{on,rev}}=-F\dd\lambda\). Substituting actual nonequilibrium work into an equilibrium identity would erase entropy production by assumption.

title: 7  Entropy, work, and thermodynamic structure
text:
7.8 Exercises and solutions
Exercise 1. Show explicitly why a zero-temperature relaxation channel need not increase diagonal entropy.






TipSolution





For probabilities \((p_0,p_1)\), full relaxation gives \((1,0)\). Starting from \((1/2,1/2)\) reduces Shannon entropy from \(\ln2\) to zero. Its population matrix has both columns equal to \((1,0)^T\); columns sum to one but rows do not. The environment receives the discarded information and energy.



Exercise 2. A three-level passive state has energies \((0,\epsilon,3\epsilon)\) and populations \((0.6,0.3,0.1)\). What work is required by the permutation exchanging levels 1 and 3?






TipSolution





Initial energy is \(0.6\epsilon\). Final populations are \((0.1,0.3,0.6)\) and final energy is \(2.1\epsilon\). Work into the system is \(1.5\epsilon\). The two cumulative deficits are both \(0.5\); Equation 7.5 gives \(\epsilon(0.5)+2\epsilon(0.5)=1.5\epsilon\).



Exercise 3. Explain why local ETH and zero diagonal entropy are compatible.






TipSolution





In a single energy eigenstate, energy measurement has one certain outcome, so \(S_d=0\). Local observables depend on a small reduced density matrix, which can be close to a thermal state because the eigenstate is entangled with the rest. Local thermality does not imply a mixed global preparation.

[2] W. Pusz and S. L. Woronowicz, Passive states and KMS states for general quantum systems, Communications in Mathematical Physics 58, 273 (1978).


[3] L. F. Santos, A. Polkovnikov, and M. Rigol, Entropy of isolated quantum systems after a quench, Physical Review Letters 107, 040601 (2011).

title: 8  Fluctuation theorems and energy diffusion
text:
8.1 Measuring work in a closed quantum system
The second law constrains averages. Fluctuation relations explain how individual realizations can return energy to a drive while the average still dissipates. Their proofs expose an important distinction: exact identities based on preparation and microscopic reversibility do not require quantum chaos, whereas replacing a thermal ensemble by one representative eigenstate requires additional structure. We retain \(k_B=1\) and count work as positive when delivered to the system.
For a protocol \(H_F(t)\) on \(0\le t\le\tau\), let \(H_i=H_F(0)\) and \(H_f=H_F(\tau)\). In the two-projective-measurement (TPM) protocol, measure the initial energy \(E_n^i\), evolve with \(U_F\), and measure the final energy \(E_m^f\). The measured work is the number
\[
W_{mn}=E_m^f-E_n^i.
\]
Work here labels a pair of outcomes; it is not generally the spectrum of one Hermitian operator. An initial energy measurement dephases a coherent state, so the resulting statistics describe that measurement procedure. A Gibbs initial state is already energy diagonal and is unaffected by this dephasing.
Write
\[
p_F(n,m)=\frac{e^{-\beta E_n^i}}{Z_i}
\abs{\bra{m,f}U_F\ket{n,i}}^2.
\tag{8.1}\]
For degeneracies, one may resolve states within each energy eigenspace or work directly with spectral projectors and their multiplicities. The projector formulation makes the same identities without choosing an arbitrary basis inside a degenerate space. An experimentally broadened histogram should retain enough resolution to compare corresponding forward and reverse bins.

title: 8  Fluctuation theorems and energy diffusion
text:
8.2 Microscopic reversibility and Crooks’ relation
Let \(\Theta\) denote the antiunitary time-reversal operator. The reversed experiment uses
\[
H_R(t)=\Theta H_F(\tau-t)\Theta^{-1},
\qquad U_R=\Theta U_F^\dagger\Theta^{-1}.
\]
All time-reversal-odd control parameters, including magnetic fields, must also reverse. Antiunitarity then implies equality of conditional transition probabilities:
\[
\abs{\bra{m,f}U_F\ket{n,i}}^2
=\abs{\bra{\Theta n,i}U_R\ket{\Theta m,f}}^2.
\]
Prepare the reverse experiment in the Gibbs state of the reversed final Hamiltonian. Dividing the two joint probabilities cancels the transition factor:
\[
\frac{p_F(n,m)}{p_R(\Theta m,\Theta n)}
=\frac{e^{-\beta E_n^i}/Z_i}{e^{-\beta E_m^f}/Z_f}
=e^{\beta(W_{mn}-\Delta F)},
\qquad \Delta F=-\beta^{-1}\ln(Z_f/Z_i).
\]
Summing over pairs with the same work gives
\[
\frac{P_F(W)}{P_R(-W)}=e^{\beta(W-\Delta F)}.
\tag{8.2}\]
Ratios are understood where the corresponding probabilities have support; distributional versions avoid dividing delta functions. This is the work fluctuation relation associated with  [1]. Quantum TPM formulations were developed, among others, by  [2]. No ETH assumption entered the proof.
Multiplication by \(e^{-\beta W}\) and integration over \(W\) immediately yields
\[
\ev{e^{-\beta W}}_F=e^{-\beta\Delta F}.
\tag{8.3}\]
The nonequilibrium work equality was introduced by  [3]. For an isolated quantum system it also follows directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ev{e^{-\beta W}}
&=\frac1{Z_i}\sum_{mn}e^{-\beta E_m^f}\abs{U_{mn}}^2\\
&=\frac1{Z_i}\sum_me^{-\beta E_m^f}=\frac{Z_f}{Z_i}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last step needs the row normalization of the transition matrix; it does not need time-reversal symmetry. Thus the equality is also valid for a trace-preserving unital channel between the two energy measurements, whereas the stated forward/reverse ratio requires a suitable reverse dynamics.
Jensen’s inequality, \(\ev{e^X}\ge e^{\ev X}\), gives \(\ev W\ge\Delta F\) for \(\beta>0\). This average bound allows individual realizations with \(W<\Delta F\). The exponential average weighs rare small-work events strongly, which can make estimating free-energy differences from finite samples difficult.






NoteSolved example: sudden reversal of a two-level field



Let \(H_i=(\epsilon/2)\sigma_z\) and \(H_f=-H_i\), with an instantaneous switch, so \(U=I\). A state initially in the lower level receives work \(+\epsilon\) and the upper state receives \(-\epsilon\). The partition functions agree. Their probabilities are
\[
p_-={e^{\beta\epsilon/2}\over2\cosh(\beta\epsilon/2)},
\qquad p_+={e^{-\beta\epsilon/2}\over2\cosh(\beta\epsilon/2)}.
\]
Consequently \(p_-e^{-\beta\epsilon}+p_+e^{\beta\epsilon}=1\). The mean work is \(\epsilon\tanh(\beta\epsilon/2)>0\), although negative work occurs with probability \(p_+\). The two outcomes, including the rare one, are essential for the equality.

text:
8.3 Work cumulants and dissipation
The logarithm of the work moment-generating function separates Gaussian and non-Gaussian contributions. If the cumulants \(\kappa_r\) exist in the required convergence domain, taking the logarithm of Equation 8.3 gives
\[
-\beta\Delta F
=-\beta\kappa_1+\frac{\beta^2}{2}\kappa_2
-\frac{\beta^3}{6}\kappa_3+\cdots.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\ev W-\Delta F
=\frac\beta2\operatorname{Var}W
-\frac{\beta^2}{6}\kappa_3+\cdots.
\]
The frequently used Gaussian relation between mean dissipated work and its variance is a truncation of this hierarchy. Small drive amplitude can control such a truncation over a specified protocol, but an apparently Gaussian central region of a histogram does not control its rare tails. Those tails are precisely where the exponential average can be most sensitive. For distributions whose moment-generating function is not analytic over the relevant interval, the exact equality should be used directly rather than through a formal cumulant series.
Crooks’ relation also gives an information-theoretic measure of irreversibility. Multiply the logarithm of Equation 8.2 by \(P_F(W)\) and integrate:
\[
D\big(P_F(W)\Vert P_R(-W)\big)
=\beta(\ev W-\Delta F)\ge0.
\]
Thus dissipated work measures how well the forward work histogram can be distinguished from the reflected reverse histogram. At the level of full trajectories, additional observed variables can retain more information than a work histogram, but under the stated work relation this particular relative entropy has exactly the displayed value. Equality means that the two work distributions coincide almost everywhere. The conclusion concerns the ensemble of outcomes, not a prohibition on any individual negative-dissipation event.

text:
8.4 A microcanonical relation and the eigenstate question
An energy shell \(a\) of \(H_i\) has projector \(\Pi_a^i\) and dimension \(g_a^i\). A shell \(b\) of \(H_f\) similarly has \(\Pi_b^f\) and dimension \(g_b^f\). Uniform preparation within a shell gives
\[
K_F(b|a)=\frac1{g_a^i}
\tr(\Pi_b^fU_F\Pi_a^iU_F^\dagger).
\]
Cyclicity of the trace and the reversed propagator imply the exact finite-shell identity
\[
g_a^iK_F(b|a)=g_b^fK_R(a|b).
\tag{8.4}\]
For narrow shells of the same width, let \(E\) and \(E+W\) denote their energies. With \(S=\ln(\Omega\delta E)\), the continuum form is
\[
\frac{P_F(W|E)}{P_R(-W|E+W)}
=\exp[S_f(E+W)-S_i(E)].
\tag{8.5}\]
This is a density-of-states relation, not a canonical work theorem with a fixed temperature. The exact quantum microcanonical formulation is discussed in  [4]. For a cyclic protocol and work small on the scale over which temperature varies,
\[
S(E+W)-S(E)=\beta(E)W
+\frac12\beta'(E)W^2+\cdots,
\qquad \beta'=-\frac1{T^2C}.
\]
The curvature term is a finite-heat-capacity correction. Even for macroscopic \(E\), it matters when work fluctuations become comparable to \(T\sqrt C\). One should not claim a fixed-\(\beta\) Jarzynski equality for every sharply prepared finite-energy state: the reverse distribution in Equation 8.5 starts at the work-dependent energy \(E+W\).
Can one replace the uniform shell by one eigenstate? Ordinary diagonal ETH controls expectation values of simple observables. A full work histogram involves \(U_F^\dagger\Pi_b^fU_F\), which can be highly nonlocal. Therefore ordinary ETH alone is insufficient for arbitrary protocols. A single-eigenstate extension is justified when the specific coarse-grained transition kernel self-averages over nearby eigenstates, as can occur for weak, physically simple driving in a chaotic system. Under that additional assumption the shell identity holds approximately for a representative eigenstate, with errors from finite shell width, finite size, and residual fluctuations. It is a controlled expectation in specified regimes, not an exact theorem for every eigenstate and every unitary.

text:
8.5 Why a bath produces detailed balance
Consider a small system with levels \(\epsilon_n\) coupled weakly to a much larger bath. If the small system changes from \(m\) to \(n\), the bath loses \(\Delta=\epsilon_n-\epsilon_m\). Pairwise microscopic transition matrix elements are related by reversibility; the number of accessible bath final states supplies the bias:
\[
\frac{w_{nm}}{w_{mn}}
\simeq\frac{\Omega_B(E_B-\Delta)}{\Omega_B(E_B)}
\simeq e^{-\beta_B\Delta}.
\tag{8.6}\]
The second step neglects bath entropy curvature and assumes its temperature is stable. Substitution shows \(w_{nm}p_m^{\mathrm{eq}}=w_{mn}p_n^{\mathrm{eq}}\) for \(p_n^{\mathrm{eq}}\propto e^{-\beta_B\epsilon_n}\). This is detailed balance, which forbids stationary probability currents on individual links. A Gibbs stationary distribution alone is a weaker condition and does not establish pairwise balance.
In a quantum weak-coupling derivation, the same factor comes from the bath’s equilibrium correlation spectrum and its KMS relation. The population master equation additionally requires suitable short bath memory and a secular approximation or other control of coherences. Strong coupling can change both the effective equilibrium state and what energy is assigned to the system.

section: 8.6 Drift, diffusion, and a finite-size Einstein relation
text:
8.6 Drift, diffusion, and a finite-size Einstein relation
Suppose many weak drive cycles produce energy increments \(\Delta E\) with short memory. Per unit coarse-grained time define
\[
A(E)=\lim_{\delta t\to0}\frac{\ev{\Delta E|E}}{\delta t},
\qquad
B(E)=\lim_{\delta t\to0}\frac{\ev{(\Delta E)^2|E}}{\delta t}.
\]
The limit is a coarse-grained diffusion limit, not the microscopic short-time limit of coherent Schrödinger evolution. Higher conditional moments must be negligible at the retained resolution. Expanding the gain and loss terms of an energy jump process to second order gives
\[
\partial_tP=-\partial_E(AP)+\frac12\partial_E^2(BP)
=-\partial_EJ,
\quad J=AP-\frac12\partial_E(BP).
\tag{8.7}\]
Here \(P(E)\dd E\) is probability in an energy interval, not probability per eigenstate. Doubly stochastic evolution preserves equal probabilities per state, which corresponds to \(P_\infty(E)\propto\Omega(E)\). If energy boundaries carry no probability current, stationarity gives
\[
0=A\Omega-\frac12\partial_E(B\Omega),
\qquad
2A(E)=B(E)\beta(E)+\partial_EB(E).
\tag{8.8}\]
This is an Einstein relation for energy space. It follows within the diffusion approximation from preservation of the density-of-states measure and zero stationary current. Reversibility provides another route through the local jump relation. The derivative term must be retained for small systems or strongly energy-dependent noise. Discarding it is a thermodynamic approximation, often of relative order \(1/N\) for smooth extensive systems, rather than an exact identity.
A bath instead selects \(P_{\mathrm{eq}}(E)\propto\Omega(E)e^{-\beta_BE}\), leading to
\[
2A=B(\beta(E)-\beta_B)+B'.
\]
Thus a colder system, with larger \(\beta\), tends to gain energy. Noise strength and dissipative drift cannot be chosen independently when the specified equilibrium measure must be preserved. The energy diffusion framework and its driven applications are developed in  [5].
Integrating Equation 8.7 over the allowed interval gives \(\dot{\mathcal P}=J(E_{\min})-J(E_{\max})\). Reflecting boundaries impose \(J=0\) and conserve probability. Absorbing boundaries describe escape and must be accompanied by a loss probability. At an unbounded high-energy end, normalizability and vanishing flux at infinity replace a fictitious finite reflecting wall. Near a ground state, a diffusion expansion can fail because individual level spacings and one-sided jumps matter. Negative temperatures are possible only for appropriate bounded spectra; the same density-of-states derivative can become negative, reversing the drift toward the entropy maximum.

title: 8  Fluctuation theorems and energy diffusion
text:
8.7 Two conserved quantities
Let two weakly coupled systems exchange energy \(q\) and particle number \(n\), positive into system 1. Their initial grand-canonical weights are proportional to \(e^{-\beta_j(E_j-\mu_jN_j)}\). Conservation makes the changes of system 2 equal \((-q,-n)\). Dividing the initial weight of a transition by that of its reverse gives
\[
\frac{P_F(q,n)}{P_R(-q,-n)}
=e^{a_Eq+a_Nn},
\quad a_E=\beta_1-\beta_2,
\quad a_N=-\beta_1\mu_1+\beta_2\mu_2.
\tag{8.9}\]
This assumes negligible coupling-energy corrections at measurement times and the appropriate reversed controls. Energy and particle transfer must be retained jointly: marginalizing over particles generally destroys a simple energy-only exponential ratio when \(a_N\ne0\).
For several continuous conserved coordinates \(x_i\), define \(B_{ij}=\ev{\Delta x_i\Delta x_j}/\delta t\). A zero-current equilibrium diffusion has
\[
2A_i=\sum_j\left[B_{ij}\partial_{x_j}S+\partial_{x_j}B_{ij}\right].
\]
A nonzero stationary divergence-free current would require a separate analysis; stationarity alone in multiple dimensions does not force every current component to vanish. Off-diagonal diffusion encodes correlations such as particles carrying energy and is the starting point for thermoelectric response.

text:
8.8 Exercises and solutions
Exercise 1. If cyclic work is Gaussian with mean \(a\) and variance \(b\), what does canonical Jarzynski imply?






TipSolution





The Gaussian moment-generating function gives \(\ev{e^{-\beta W}}=e^{-\beta a+\beta^2b/2}\). For \(\Delta F=0\), this equals one, so \(2a=\beta b\). Non-Gaussian cumulants correct this formula; it is not the complete finite-size energy-diffusion relation when the noise depends on initial energy.



Exercise 2. For \(\Omega(E)\propto E^{\alpha-1}\) and \(B(E)=bE\), find the isolated drift.






TipSolution





Here \(\beta=(\alpha-1)/E\) and \(B'=b\). Equation Equation 8.8 gives \(A=b\alpha/2\). Omitting \(B'\) would incorrectly replace \(\alpha\) by \(\alpha-1\) and can even predict zero heating for a constant density of states.



Exercise 3. Two systems have equal temperatures but different chemical potentials. Can their energy transfers have an unbiased distribution?






TipSolution





Equal temperatures set \(a_E=0\), but \(a_N=\beta(\mu_2-\mu_1)\) remains. The joint distribution is biased in particle transfer, and particle-energy correlations can bias the energy marginal. Equal temperatures alone do not remove chemical work.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
text:
9.1 Linear response from the von Neumann equation
A weak probe measures both how a system fluctuates and how it reacts. In equilibrium these measurements are linked by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. The connection becomes especially interesting in an isolated chaotic system: a single energy eigenstate is stationary, yet its matrix elements can encode the same local noise and response as a thermal ensemble. This chapter derives the relations with explicit conventions, then explains what ETH adds and what it does not.
Take Hermitian observables \(A\) and \(B\), a stationary initial state \([\rho_0,H_0]=0\), and a perturbation
\[
H(t)=H_0-f(t)B.
\]
The minus sign defines our convention for the applied field. In the interaction picture,
\[
\dot\rho_I=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[-f(t)B_I(t),\rho_I(t)].
\]
Keeping one power of \(f\) and integrating from the remote past gives
\[
\delta\rho_I(t)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^t
\dd t'\,f(t')[B_I(t'),\rho_0].
\]
Taking the trace with \(A_I(t)\) and moving operators cyclically inside the trace yields
\[
\delta\ev{A(t)}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dd t'\,
\chi_{AB}(t-t')f(t'),
\qquad
\chi_{AB}(t)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\theta(t)
\ev{[A(t),B(0)]}_0.
\tag{9.1}\]
This is the retarded Kubo formula. It holds for any stationary state, including an individual eigenstate; thermal equilibrium is not needed for its derivation. The step function expresses causality. Kubo’s general response formulation is developed in  [1].
We use angular frequency and Fourier transforms
\[
X(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dd t\,e^{i\omega t}X(t),
\qquad
X(t)=\int\frac{\dd\omega}{2\pi}e^{-i\omega t}X(\omega).
\]
For a monochromatic field, \(\delta A(\omega)=\chi_{AB}(\omega)f(\omega)\). If the observable itself depends explicitly on the field, its derivative contributes an additional instantaneous term. Conductivity calculations, for example, must keep the appropriate diamagnetic contribution rather than applying the commutator term to an incomplete observable.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
text:
9.2 Causality and dispersive response
A further relation follows from causality without invoking equilibrium. Because \(\chi_{AB}(t)\) vanishes at negative time, its Fourier transform is analytic for \(\operatorname{Im}\omega>0\) when the response decays sufficiently fast. A small positive imaginary part of frequency is also the prescription for switching on a probe adiabatically. For a scalar response that falls off at large frequency, contour integration then gives the Kramers–Kronig relations
\[
\chi'(\omega)=\frac1\pi\mathcal P\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{\chi''(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega',
\qquad
\chi''(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\mathcal P\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{\chi'(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'.
\]
The symbol \(\mathcal P\) denotes the symmetric principal value around the pole. Instantaneous terms or nondecaying high-frequency pieces require a subtraction before applying these formulas. In practice the relations check whether measured absorption and dispersion can belong to one causal response.
For Hermitian \(A=B\), the time-domain response is real, so \(\chi(-\omega)=\chi(\omega)^*\): the real part is even and the imaginary part is odd. In particular, when the integral converges,
\[
\chi'(0)=\frac2\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{\chi''(\omega')}{\omega'}\dd\omega'.
\]
This is a relation between response components. It is logically distinct from FDT, which relates response to fluctuations and requires the extra spectral balance condition. A stationary nonequilibrium state can obey causality and the dispersion relations while violating thermal FDT. Likewise, a vanishing absorption at one frequency says nothing by itself about the temperature or the total noise at other frequencies.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
text:
9.3 Spectral noise and detailed balance
Define the connected, ordered correlation and its spectrum by
\[
C_{AB}(t)=\ev{\delta A(t)\delta B(0)},
\qquad
C_{AB}(\omega)=\int\dd t\,e^{i\omega t}C_{AB}(t),
\]
where \(\delta A=A-\ev A\). For \(\rho_0=\sum_np_n\ket n\bra n\), inserting a complete energy basis gives, away from the subtracted static piece,
\[
C_{AB}(\omega)=2\pi\sum_{nm}p_nA_{nm}B_{mn}
\delta\left(\omega-\frac{E_m-E_n}{\hbar}\right).
\tag{9.2}\]
With this convention positive frequency corresponds to transitions in which the system absorbs energy \(\hbar\omega\). For \(A=B\), the spectrum is nonnegative. It can be strongly asymmetric between positive and negative frequency: emission and absorption are different quantum processes.
In a Gibbs state \(p_m/p_n=e^{-\beta(E_m-E_n)}\). Exchanging the indices in the negative-frequency spectrum therefore gives
\[
C_{BA}(-\omega)=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}C_{AB}(\omega).
\tag{9.3}\]
This is the spectral detailed-balance or KMS relation. For a cross spectrum it exchanges both frequency and observable order. Replacing it by an evenness statement for \(C_{AB}\) would discard quantum ordering and can be wrong even at equilibrium.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
text:
9.4 The fluctuation-dissipation theorem
For a matrix of responses, define its dissipative part by
\[
\chi_{AB}^{\mathrm d}(\omega)
=\frac{\chi_{AB}(\omega)-\chi_{BA}(\omega)^*}{2i}.
\]
For a single observable this reduces to \(\chi''_{AA}=\Im\chi_{AA}\). The Fourier transform of the full commutator in Equation 9.1 gives
\[
\chi_{AB}^{\mathrm d}(\omega)
=\frac{C_{AB}(\omega)-C_{BA}(-\omega)}{2\hbar}.
\]
Define the symmetrized spectrum
\[
C_{AB}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\omega)
=\frac12\left[C_{AB}(\omega)+C_{BA}(-\omega)\right].
\]
Using Equation 9.3 to eliminate the negative-frequency term yields
\[
C_{AB}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\omega)
=\hbar\coth\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega}{2}\right)
\chi_{AB}^{\mathrm d}(\omega).
\tag{9.4}\]
For scalar autocorrelations this is the familiar equilibrium fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Its low-frequency classical limit, \(\beta\hbar\abs\omega\ll1\), is
\[
C_{AA}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\omega)
\simeq\frac{2T}{\omega}\chi''_{AA}(\omega).
\]
At \(T=0\), quantum fluctuations remain and the hyperbolic cotangent tends to the sign of \(\omega\). The product has a finite positive autocorrelation spectrum. A positive-temperature passive state has \(\chi''_{AA}(\omega)\ge0\) for \(\omega>0\). A bounded-spectrum negative-temperature state can instead provide gain; its population inversion changes the sign of the absorptive response.
For \(f(t)=f_0\cos\omega t\) coupled as \(-fA\), the average input power over a cycle is
\[
\overline{\dot W}=\frac12f_0^2\omega\chi''_{AA}(\omega).
\]
To verify the sign, write the response as \(f_0[\chi'\cos\omega t+\chi''\sin\omega t]\) and average \(-\dot f\,\delta\ev A\). Positive \(\chi''\) therefore represents heating in our convention. Reversing either the Fourier convention or the sign of the coupling changes intermediate signs, so these definitions should always accompany a response formula.






NoteSolved example: an oscillator spectrum



For \(H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega_0^2x^2/2\), let \(x=x_0(a+a^\dagger)\) with \(x_0^2=\hbar/(2m\omega_0)\). Thermal occupation is \(\bar n=(e^{\beta\hbar\omega_0}-1)^{-1}\). Direct calculation gives
\[
C_{xx}(\omega)=2\pi x_0^2\left[(\bar n+1)\delta(\omega-\omega_0)
+\bar n\delta(\omega+\omega_0)\right].
\]
The ratio of negative- to positive-frequency weights is \(\bar n/(\bar n+1)=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_0}\). The commutator eliminates \(\bar n\), giving
\[
\chi''_{xx}(\omega)=\frac{\pi}{2m\omega_0}
[\delta(\omega-\omega_0)-\delta(\omega+\omega_0)].
\]
The symmetrized noise retains the factor \(2\bar n+1=\coth(\beta\hbar\omega_0/2)\), exactly as in Equation 9.4. This integrable example also emphasizes that canonical FDT itself does not require chaos.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
section: 9.5 How an eigenstate can satisfy thermal FDT
text:
9.5 How an eigenstate can satisfy thermal FDT
For one eigenstate \(\ket n\), the exact spectrum is
\[
C_{AA}^{(n)}(\omega)=2\pi\sum_{m\ne n}\abs{A_{nm}}^2
\delta\left(\omega-\frac{E_m-E_n}{\hbar}\right).
\]
Its upward and downward transition weights are not related by Gibbs probabilities, since only one initial state is occupied. Off-diagonal ETH supplies a different mechanism. Write its smooth variance schematically as
\[
\overline{\abs{A_{nm}}^2}
=e^{-S(\bar E)}\abs{f_A(\bar E,\varepsilon)}^2,
\quad \bar E=(E_n+E_m)/2,
\quad\varepsilon=E_m-E_n.
\]
An energy reference in \(S\) and the units of \(f_A\) must be chosen consistently; it cancels in the following ratio. Hermiticity makes the smooth variance even in \(\varepsilon\). Replacing the sum by a density-of-states integral after suitable frequency smoothing gives
\[
C_{AA}^{(n)}(\omega)\propto
\Omega(E_n+\hbar\omega)
e^{-S(E_n+\hbar\omega/2)}
\abs{f_A(E_n+\hbar\omega/2,\hbar\omega)}^2.
\]
Set \(\varepsilon=\hbar\omega\) and expand the logarithm of the ratio at fixed microscopic \(\varepsilon\):
\[
\ln\frac{C_{AA}^{(n)}(-\omega)}{C_{AA}^{(n)}(\omega)}
=-\beta(E_n)\varepsilon
-\varepsilon\,\partial_E\ln\abs{f_A(E_n,\varepsilon)}^2
+O(\varepsilon^3\partial_E^3S,\varepsilon^3\partial_E^3\ln\abs f_A^2).
\tag{9.5}\]
The density of accessible final states contributes \(-2\beta\varepsilon\); the ETH matrix-element envelope contributes \(+\beta\varepsilon\). Their combination produces the thermal factor. For a smooth local-observable envelope depending on energy density, its logarithmic derivative is generally \(O(1/N)\) at fixed frequency. Thus thermal detailed balance and FDT emerge to leading thermodynamic order with temperature fixed by the eigenstate energy. This is an ETH consequence, whereas the exact Kubo formula for that eigenstate required only stationarity. Connections between chaotic matrix elements, relaxation, and equilibrium correlation functions were developed in  [2].
The order of limits matters. A finite isolated system has discrete lines and recurrences. One needs frequency windows containing many transitions, yet narrow relative to physical spectral features, or observation times below the recurrence scale. At very low frequencies, hydrodynamic modes and conservation laws can create structure that a naive smooth-envelope expansion misses. The approximation also fails when the energy difference probes a finite fraction of the total energy, or where ETH itself fails.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
text:
9.6 Two-observable ETH requires joint information
Separate ETH fits for \(A\) and \(B\) do not determine \(C_{AB}\). One needs the smooth joint covariance
\[
g_{AB}(\bar E,\varepsilon)
=e^{S(\bar E)}\overline{A_{nm}B_{mn}}.
\]
The fluctuating parts of different observables cannot generally be treated as independent random numbers. Their covariance retains conserved overlaps, selection rules, phases, and possible time-reversal parity. For every vector of complex coefficients \(v_A\), the matrix of positive-frequency ordered spectra obeys
\[
\sum_{AB}v_A^*C_{AB}(\omega)v_B\ge0,
\]
because it is the noise spectrum of the corresponding linear combination. In particular,
\[
\abs{C_{AB}(\omega)}^2\le C_{AA}(\omega)C_{BB}(\omega).
\]
A joint ETH description consistent with this positivity and microscopic symmetries reproduces the cross-observable version of Equation 9.4 after the same smoothing and thermodynamic limits. Autocorrelation ETH alone leaves the cross spectrum undetermined.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
text:
9.7 Onsager–Casimir reciprocity
Let \(x_i\) be slowly exchanged extensive coordinates and \(a_i\) their thermodynamic affinities, normalized so entropy production is \(\dot S=\sum_i a_iJ_i\), where \(J_i=\dot x_i\). Near equilibrium,
\[
\ev{J_i}=\sum_jL_{ij}a_j+O(a^2).
\]
An energy affinity is an inverse-temperature difference; a particle affinity includes \(-\beta\mu\). The symmetric part of \(L\) must be positive semidefinite, since \(\sum_{ij}a_iL_{ij}a_j\ge0\). The antisymmetric part produces no entropy to this order.
Suppose time reversal sends \(x_i\to\epsilon_i x_i\), with \(\epsilon_i=\pm1\), and reverses magnetic field \(\mathcal B\). Microscopic reversibility relates the corresponding equilibrium current correlations. In a classical reversible setting, or with quantum correlations replaced by the appropriate Kubo-transformed correlations, integrating this relation gives
\[
L_{ij}(\mathcal B)=\epsilon_i\epsilon_jL_{ji}(-\mathcal B).
\tag{9.6}\]
The Kubo transform can be written as
\[
C_{ij}^{K}(t)=\frac1\beta\int_0^\beta\dd u\,
\ev{J_j(-i\hbar u)J_i(t)}_{\mathrm{eq}}.
\]
For entropy-normalized affinities, a Green–Kubo expression has the form \(L_{ij}=\int_0^\infty C_{ij}^{K}(t)\dd t\), with volume and geometry factors determined by whether \(J_i\) is a total current or a current density. In a system without magnetic fields and for variables of the same parity, Equation 9.6 reduces to \(L_{ij}=L_{ji}\). For example, the response of particle flow to a temperature affinity equals the reciprocal energy-flow response to the corresponding particle affinity, once both forces and currents use conjugate normalizations. Comparing coefficients defined with different temperature factors can hide this equality.

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
section: 9.8 Nonlinear relations from a fluctuation symmetry
text:
9.8 Nonlinear relations from a fluctuation symmetry
Fluctuation relations contain information beyond linear response. For one integrated transfer \(Q\) in time \(t\), assume the steady-state large-time statistics satisfy \(P_a(Q)/P_a(-Q)=e^{aQ}\) at zero magnetic field, up to boundary corrections subextensive in \(t\). Define
\[
g(\lambda,a)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\ln\ev{e^{-\lambda Q}}_a
=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{(-\lambda)^r}{r!}c_r(a).
\]
Here \(c_1\) is the mean current and \(c_2\) is the growth rate of its variance. The probability symmetry gives
\[
g(\lambda,a)=g(a-\lambda,a),\qquad g(0,a)=g(a,a)=0.
\tag{9.7}\]
Expansion at \(\lambda=a\) therefore implies
\[
c_1(a)=\frac a2c_2(a)-\frac{a^2}{6}c_3(a)
+\frac{a^3}{24}c_4(a)+\cdots.
\]
At equilibrium, odd cumulants vanish. If \(c_1=La+Ma^2/2+\cdots\) and \(c_2=C_0+C_1a+\cdots\), coefficient matching gives
\[
L=\frac12C_0,\qquad M=C_1.
\tag{9.8}\]
The first equality is a zero-frequency fluctuation-dissipation relation. The second ties a nonlinear current coefficient to the first change of noise with affinity. Higher orders involve higher cumulants and their derivatives; there is no general license to discard them. For several affinities one differentiates the vector version of Equation 9.7. Magnetic-field reversal must be included in that symmetry before deriving nonlinear parity relations, as illustrated by  [3].

title: 9  Response, fluctuations, and reciprocity
text:
9.9 Exercises and solutions
Exercise 1. At \(\beta\hbar\omega=\ln3\), what is the ratio of emission to absorption noise for a thermal Hermitian observable?






TipSolution





With our frequency convention, emission is the negative-frequency spectrum. Its ratio to absorption is \(e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}=1/3\). The symmetrized spectrum is not the same as either ordered spectrum.



Exercise 2. Why does causality alone not imply thermal FDT for a pure eigenstate?






TipSolution





Causality yields the retarded commutator response and relates its real and imaginary parts. FDT additionally requires a relation between the commutator and the symmetric fluctuations. A generic eigenstate has no Gibbs KMS identity; ETH can supply an approximate spectral balance for suitable observables and frequency windows.



Exercise 3. A current has \(c_2(a)=4+6a+O(a^2)\). Find its first two response coefficients under the stated fluctuation symmetry.






TipSolution





Equation Equation 9.8 gives \(L=2\) and \(M=6\), so \(c_1(a)=2a+3a^2+O(a^3)\). These numbers refer to the entropy affinity \(a\); converting to a voltage or temperature difference may introduce additional factors.







[1] R. Kubo, Statistical-mechanical theory of irreversible processes. I. General theory and simple applications to magnetic and conduction problems, Journal of the Physical Society of Japan 12, 570 (1957).


[2] M. Srednicki, The approach to thermal equilibrium in quantized chaotic systems, Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General 32, 1163 (1999).


[3] K. Saito and Y. Utsumi, Symmetry in full counting statistics, fluctuation theorem, and relations among nonlinear transport coefficients in the presence of a magnetic field, Physical Review B 78, 115429 (2008).

title: 10  Driven systems and finite reservoirs
text:
10.1 A particle in a moving chaotic cavity
The energy-space Einstein relation becomes useful when microscopic driving is complicated but its scaling with energy is simple. It determines the noise from a measured heating rate and a density of states, or conversely predicts heating from fluctuations. We now work through three applications: a particle accelerated by a moving chaotic boundary, a harmonic probe kicked while attached to a finite equilibrating system, and two finite bodies exchanging energy. The distributions below are consequences of stated continuum models; they are not numerical evidence that every microscopic drive realizes those models.
A particle of mass \(m\) has kinetic energy \(E=mv^2/2\) in a \(d\)-dimensional cavity. Assume that the fixed-wall billiard mixes its collision angles sufficiently quickly. The wall moves slowly, with normal velocity \(u\) much smaller than a typical particle speed. Locally specular reflection in the wall frame gives
\[
v_n'=2u-v_n,\qquad
\Delta E=2mu^2-2muv_n.
\]
The fluctuating term is first order in \(u\), while its mean vanishes for an unbiased wall velocity before accounting for collision sampling. The positive quadratic term and the bias of collision sampling both contribute to the mean. Their precise coefficient depends on geometry and wall statistics. Their energy scaling follows without solving trajectories: collision rate is proportional to \(v/L\), so
\[
A(E)\propto\frac{mu^2v}{L}\propto E^{1/2},
\qquad
B(E)\propto\frac{m^2u^2v^3}{L}\propto E^{3/2}.
\]
The required assumptions are weak energy change per collision, short correlations on the heating time, and no slowly trapped family of trajectories dominating the statistics. A classically chaotic shape alone does not guarantee every one of these assumptions for every boundary motion. Coherent quantum interference can also invalidate a classical diffusion picture over sufficiently long times.
Weyl counting gives \(\Omega(E)\propto E^{d/2-1}\) in the semiclassical regime, so \(\beta=(d/2-1)/E\). Parameterize the diffusion strength by \(b>0\):
\[
B(E)=bE^{3/2}.
\]
Retaining the finite-system derivative in the Einstein relation gives
\[
A(E)=\frac12\left[B\beta+B'\right]
=\frac{b(d+1)}4\sqrt E.
\tag{10.1}\]
The derivative is essential for a single particle. In \(d=2\), the density of states is constant and \(\beta=0\), yet heating remains positive. A naive equation \(2A=B\beta\) would miss it completely.

title: 10  Driven systems and finite reservoirs
text:
10.2 Solving the cavity diffusion model
Use the Itô stochastic equation equivalent to the Fokker–Planck description:
\[
\dd E=\frac{b(d+1)}4\sqrt E\,\dd t
+\sqrt b\,E^{3/4}\dd W_t,
\qquad \ev{(\dd W_t)^2}=\dd t.
\]
The variable \(x=\sqrt E\) simplifies both coefficients. Itô’s rule includes the second derivative term:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dd x
&=\frac1{2\sqrt E}\dd E
-\frac1{8E^{3/2}}(\dd E)^2\\
&=\frac{bd}{8}\dd t+\frac{\sqrt b}{2}\sqrt x\,\dd W_t.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.2}\]
This square-root diffusion has a simple similarity solution. Let \(p_x(x,t)\) be its density with respect to \(\dd x\). For the idealized entrance law starting at \(x=0\), substitution in its Fokker–Planck equation verifies
\[
p_x(x,t)=\frac{x^{d-1}e^{-x/\vartheta}}{\Gamma(d)\vartheta^d},
\qquad \vartheta=\frac{bt}{8},\quad x\ge0.
\]
The gamma-function identity \(\int_0^\infty x^{d-1}e^{-x/\vartheta}\dd x=\Gamma(d)\vartheta^d\) normalizes it. In an actual cavity the diffusion approximation fails sufficiently near the lowest quantum levels and at speeds comparable to \(u\). A finite initial distribution instead approaches the displayed similarity shape once its initial energy scale becomes negligible, provided the continuum assumptions remain valid.
Changing variables back requires the Jacobian \(\dd x/\dd E=1/(2\sqrt E)\):
\[
P(E,t)=\frac{E^{(d-2)/2}}{2\Gamma(d)\vartheta^d}
\exp\left(-\frac{\sqrt E}{\vartheta}\right).
\tag{10.3}\]
The tail is exponential in speed, rather than in energy. This is a nonequilibrium similarity distribution; its continuing motion to higher energy rules out a stationary Gibbs interpretation. Gamma moments give
\[
\ev E=d(d+1)\vartheta^2,
\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{Var}E}{\ev{E}^2}
=\frac{4d+6}{d(d+1)}.
\tag{10.4}\]
At the same mean energy, a canonical free particle has relative variance \(2/d\). The driven distribution is therefore broader. For a rapidly internally equilibrating gas, an analogous total-energy description replaces the number of quadratic momentum coordinates by their total count. Independent particles that fail to equilibrate do not justify that replacement for the full many-particle state, even if their total energy happens to look Gaussian.






Figure 10.1: Analytic examples of energy distributions. Left: the continuum cavity model in three dimensions, with \(b=1\), showing the entrance-law solution at three times. Right: the exact equilibrium energy fraction of two finite reservoirs with density-of-states exponents \(c_1=c_2=3\). These are calculated model curves, not microscopic simulation data.



A broader driven distribution can nevertheless have the same thermodynamic entropy density as a canonical distribution. For a distribution over states represented by \(P(E)\), its coarse entropy uses the measure \(P(E)/\Omega(E)\):
\[
S[P]=-\int\dd E\,P(E)\ln\frac{P(E)}{\Omega(E)}.
\]
At fixed normalization and mean energy, maximizing this functional by Lagrange multipliers gives \(P_{\mathrm{G}}(E)\propto\Omega(E)e^{-\beta E}\). Direct substitution then gives the exact comparison
\[
S[P_{\mathrm{G}}]-S[P]=\int\dd E\,P(E)\ln\frac{P(E)}{P_{\mathrm{G}}(E)}\ge0.
\]
The inequality is relative entropy positivity. It does not determine whether the difference is extensive; that depends on whether only a collective energy distribution differs or whether independent microscopic sectors each retain extra information.

section: 10.3 A kicked harmonic probe inside a finite system
text:
10.3 A kicked harmonic probe inside a finite system
Consider a classical harmonic coordinate with
\[
\varepsilon(x,p)=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac{kx^2}{2}.
\]
Couple it weakly to a much larger but finite chaotic system, and call the total energy \(E\). Wait between kicks long enough for the probe to equilibrate internally with that system, while the total energy changes little per cycle. Its pre-kick marginal is then approximately canonical at \(T(E)\). During a very short impulse the coupling and coordinate motion are negligible. An impulse \(I(x)\) changes \(p\to p+I(x)\), and hence
\[
\Delta E=\frac{pI(x)}m+\frac{I(x)^2}{2m}.
\]
The equilibrium Gaussian momentum is independent of \(x\), has zero mean, and satisfies \(\ev{p^2}=mT\). For kicks separated by time \(\tau\), the leading drift and variance rate are consequently
\[
A(E)=\frac{\ev{I(x)^2}}{2m\tau},
\qquad
B(E)=\frac{T(E)\ev{I(x)^2}}{m\tau}=2T(E)A(E).
\tag{10.5}\]
In the variance, terms of order \(I^4\) have been dropped; the retained noise is the square of the term linear in impulse. These expressions use a canonical probe marginal and thus omit finite-reservoir corrections. The exact energy-space relation restores the \(B'\) correction, consistently of the same order as corrections to that marginal.
For example, choose \(I(x)=g\operatorname{sgn}(x)\abs x^r\) with \(r\ge0\). The position variance is \(T/k\), and a Gaussian integral gives
\[
\ev{I^2}=g^2\left(\frac{2T}{k}\right)^r
\frac{\Gamma(r+1/2)}{\sqrt\pi}.
\]
Thus different spatial profiles change how the heating rate grows with temperature. This is a useful concrete realization of the general energy-distribution framework of  [1]; the following moment calculation is independent of the oscillator details.

title: 10  Driven systems and finite reservoirs
text:
10.4 A transition in fluctuation growth
Suppose over the energy range of interest
\[
\begin{gathered}
\beta(E)=cE^{-\alpha},\qquad A(E)=aE^s,\\
a,c>0,\qquad\alpha>0.
\end{gathered}
\]
For the harmonic impulse above, \(s=\alpha r\). The mean energy \(\mu\) and variance \(v\) obey the exact diffusion moment identities, when boundary terms vanish,
\[
\dot\mu=\ev{A},\qquad
\dot v=\ev B+2\operatorname{Cov}(E,A).
\]
If the energy distribution remains narrow and higher cumulants are controlled, expand the smooth coefficients around \(\mu\). To leading order,
\[
\dot\mu=A(\mu),\qquad
\dot v=B(\mu)+2A'(\mu)v.
\]
Using the thermodynamic approximation \(B\simeq2A/\beta\) and eliminating time gives
\[
\frac{\dd v}{\dd\mu}-\frac{2s}{\mu}v
=\frac2c\mu^\alpha.
\]
The integrating factor is \(\mu^{-2s}\), so
\[
v(\mu)=\mu^{2s}\left[
\frac{v_0}{\mu_0^{2s}}
+\frac2c\int_{\mu_0}^{\mu}z^{\alpha-2s}\dd z
\right].
\tag{10.6}\]
The canonical variance at the same mean is
\[
v_{\mathrm{can}}=-\frac{\dd E}{\dd\beta}
=\frac{\mu^{1+\alpha}}{c\alpha}.
\]
Let \(\eta=2s-\alpha-1\). The elementary integral in Equation 10.6 has three qualitatively different limits:



Condition
Asymptotic comparison, for negligible initial width




\(\eta<0\)
\(v/v_{\mathrm{can}}\to2\alpha/\abs\eta\)


\(\eta=0\)
\(v/v_{\mathrm{can}}\sim2\alpha\ln(\mu/\mu_0)\)


\(\eta>0\)
\(v/v_{\mathrm{can}}\) grows proportionally to \(\mu^\eta\)



For \(\eta<0\), newly generated fluctuations dominate and the initial width becomes irrelevant. For \(\eta>0\), amplification of fluctuations generated early in the protocol dominates: the lower integration limit retains memory. At the boundary the integral is logarithmic. This is a transition in asymptotic fluctuation growth, rather than a claim of an equilibrium singularity in a partition function. Near \(\eta=0\), large \(\abs{\eta}\ln(\mu/\mu_0)\) is needed to distinguish a power from a logarithm, so long crossovers are expected.
The mean grows as
\[
\mu(t)=\left[\mu_0^{1-s}+(1-s)at\right]^{1/(1-s)}
\]
for \(s\ne1\), and as \(\mu_0e^{at}\) for \(s=1\). For \(s>1\) this ideal power-law equation diverges at finite time; microscopic weak-drive assumptions generally fail before interpreting that divergence literally. For the runaway-width regime, one must also monitor \(v/\mu^2\): once it is no longer small, the narrow-distribution closure cannot establish the subsequent full distribution. For a fixed-duration weak kick to remain small relative to the energy at arbitrarily high energy, its mean relative change \(A(E)\tau/E\propto E^{s-1}\) must not grow; this favors \(s\le1\). Under that restriction, the growing-ratio regime \(\eta>0\) requires \(\alpha<1\). A large system does not by itself guarantee Gaussian statistics at arbitrarily long times.






NoteSolved example: tuning a kick profile



Take \(\alpha=1/2\), for which \(T\propto\sqrt E\), and the harmonic probe impulse exponent \(r\). Then \(s=r/2\) and \(\eta=r-3/2\). A linear impulse (\(r=1\)) gives \(v/v_{\mathrm{can}}\to2\). At \(r=3/2\) the ratio grows logarithmically. At \(r=2\) it grows as \(\mu^{1/2}\) within the interval where the approximations remain controlled. A feedback or force profile changes noise amplification without changing the equilibrium density of states.

title: 10  Driven systems and finite reservoirs
text:
10.5 Two finite bodies exchanging energy
Now switch off the drive. Two internally equilibrating bodies have total energy \(E_{\mathrm{tot}}\), weak coupling, and subsystem energy \(E\) in body 1. The combined isolated system assigns equal probability to states at fixed total energy, so
\[
P_{\mathrm{eq}}(E)=\frac1{\mathcal Z}
\Omega_1(E)\Omega_2(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-E).
\tag{10.7}\]
The effective entropy derivative along the energy exchange coordinate is
\[
\partial_ES_{\mathrm{tot}}(E)=\beta_1(E)-\beta_2(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-E).
\]
A zero-current diffusion preserving this distribution must satisfy
\[
2A(E)=B(E)[\beta_1(E)-\beta_2(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-E)]+B'(E).
\tag{10.8}\]
If body 1 is colder, its larger inverse temperature gives a positive leading drift: it gains energy. At finite size, a nonconstant diffusion coefficient contributes the additional drift \(B'/2\); the location where mean drift vanishes need not exactly equal the mode of the stationary probability density. Energy-exchange fluctuation dynamics for finite systems is studied in  [2].
Expand the total entropy about an interior maximum \(E_*\). To quadratic order,
\[
P_{\mathrm{eq}}(E)\propto
\exp\left[-\frac{(E-E_*)^2}{2v_*}\right],
\qquad
v_*=-\frac1{S_{\mathrm{tot}}''(E_*)}
=T^2\frac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}.
\tag{10.9}\]
Both temperatures agree at the maximum. The reciprocal heat capacities add because energy entering one body leaves the other. An infinite bath, \(C_2\to\infty\), recovers \(v_*=T^2C_1\). For two equal finite bodies, the fluctuations are half that bath-limit value.
When \(B\) varies negligibly across this narrow peak, linearization yields an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process,
\[
\dd(E-E_*)=-\kappa(E-E_*)\dd t+\sqrt{B_*}\dd W_t,
\quad \kappa=\frac{B_*}{2v_*}.
\]
Its mean relaxes as \(e^{-\kappa t}\) and variance satisfies
\[
v(t)=v_*+[v(0)-v_*]e^{-2\kappa t}.
\]
Mean relaxation and noise growth therefore provide independent measurements of the same local transport coefficient. The conditions of internal equilibration, small exchange increments, and weak coupling are crucial; a few coherent coupled levels can instead exchange energy periodically.

title: 10  Driven systems and finite reservoirs
text:
10.6 An exact finite-reservoir distribution
A useful model avoids the Gaussian approximation. Let \(\Omega_i(E_i)\propto E_i^{c_i-1}\) for positive \(c_i\). The energy fraction \(u=E/E_{\mathrm{tot}}\) has the beta distribution
\[
P(u)=\frac{u^{c_1-1}(1-u)^{c_2-1}}
{\mathrm B(c_1,c_2)},\quad 0<u<1,
\qquad \mathrm B(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}.
\]
Its exact moments are
\[
\ev u=\frac{c_1}{c_1+c_2},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}u=\frac{c_1c_2}{(c_1+c_2)^2(c_1+c_2+1)}.
\]
For \(c_1,c_2>1\), its mode is \((c_1-1)/(c_1+c_2-2)\), which differs from its mean at finite size. The mode equalizes the derivatives of the two surface entropies. For large \(c_i\), this distinction is relatively small and the Gaussian heat-capacity formula follows. For \(c_1=c_2=3\), \(P(u)=30u^2(1-u)^2\), as plotted in Figure 10.1. The finite support and the vanishing probabilities at both endpoints are physical consequences of the available states in both bodies.

10.7 Exercises and solutions
Exercise 1. For the cavity model, verify \(\dd\ev E/\dd t=\ev A(E)\) using the similarity distribution.






TipSolution





Since \(\ev{\sqrt E}=d\vartheta\) and \(\dot\vartheta=b/8\), differentiating \(d(d+1)\vartheta^2\) gives \(bd(d+1)\vartheta/4\). Averaging Equation 10.1 gives the same result. Replacing \(\ev{\sqrt E}\) by \(\sqrt{\ev E}\) would not be exact for this broad one-particle distribution.



Exercise 2. For \(\alpha=1\), \(s=0\), compare driven and canonical energy variances at large mean energy.






TipSolution





Here \(\eta=-2\), so \(v/v_{\mathrm{can}}\to1\). Equality of the variance alone does not prove that the complete energy distribution or the quantum state is Gibbs.



Exercise 3. Two reservoirs have \(c_1=c_2=3\). Find their exact relative energy-fraction variance and compare with a Gaussian description.






TipSolution





The mean fraction is \(1/2\) and variance is \(9/(36\cdot7)=1/28\). The distribution is visibly non-Gaussian for these small exponents. The entropy curvature at the mode gives a local Gaussian variance \(1/16\), illustrating that a peak-curvature approximation need not reproduce the exact variance of a broad finite distribution.

title: 11  Integrability and constrained equilibrium
text:
11.1 Maximum entropy with many constraints
An isolated system can relax while remembering much more than its energy. A free gas supplies the simplest example: particles redistribute in space, but each single-particle mode keeps its occupation. An interacting integrable chain has a more elaborate version of this memory. Statistical mechanics remains useful, provided we retain the conserved information that local measurements can detect.
By the end of this chapter you should be able to construct a generalized Gibbs ensemble, compute its free-particle correlations, explain why a bosonic observable can relax in a fermionized model, and identify the missing-information problem in interacting integrable systems. We set \(k_B=1\) and use \(\hbar=1\) in time evolution.
Let \(Q_\alpha\) be Hermitian conserved operators, \([H,Q_\alpha]=0\), and let their initial expectation values be \(q_\alpha\). For now assume the charges commute with one another. We seek a density operator with these expectations and the largest von Neumann entropy. Vary
\[
-\tr(\rho\ln\rho)-\lambda_0(\tr\rho-1)
-\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha(\tr\rho Q_\alpha-q_\alpha).
\]
Using \(\delta\tr(\rho\ln\rho)=\tr[\delta\rho(\ln\rho+1)]\) gives
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{GGE}}=\frac{1}{Z}
\exp\left(-\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha Q_\alpha\right),
\qquad Z=\tr\exp\left(-\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha Q_\alpha\right).
\tag{11.1}\]
The multipliers satisfy \(q_\alpha=-\partial_{\lambda_\alpha}\ln Z\). Their susceptibility matrix is the charge covariance matrix, \(\partial_{\lambda_\alpha}\partial_{\lambda_\beta}\ln Z=\ev{Q_\alpha Q_\beta}-\ev{Q_\alpha}\ev{Q_\beta}\), which is positive semidefinite. Redundant charges can therefore make the multipliers nonunique even when the state is unique.
There is also a useful proof of maximality. For any other state \(\sigma\) satisfying the same constraints, positivity of quantum relative entropy gives
\[
0\leq D(\sigma\Vert\rho_{\mathrm{GGE}})
=-S(\sigma)+\ln Z+\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha q_\alpha
=S(\rho_{\mathrm{GGE}})-S(\sigma).
\]
This is a variational result, not a dynamical theorem. It does not prove that unitary evolution approaches the GGE. Nor does it say which charges suffice. Including every eigenstate projector reproduces the diagonal ensemble exactly but gives little compression. The physical question is whether local and quasilocal conserved quantities determine the state seen by every fixed finite subsystem. Early hard-core-boson calculations established the practical usefulness of this idea  [1].

title: 11  Integrability and constrained equilibrium
section: 11.2 Free fermions: occupations, correlations, and dephasing
text:
11.2 Free fermions: occupations, correlations, and dephasing
Consider a number-conserving quadratic Hamiltonian on \(L\) sites,
\[
H=\sum_{ij}h_{ij}c_i^\dagger c_j
=\sum_\mu\epsilon_\mu d_\mu^\dagger d_\mu,
\qquad c_i=\sum_\mu\phi_\mu(i)d_\mu.
\]
The anticommutation rules are \(\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}\) and \(\{c_i,c_j\}=0\). Each \(I_\mu=d_\mu^\dagger d_\mu\) has eigenvalues 0 and 1 and commutes with \(H\). Constraining \(n_\mu=\ev{I_\mu}_0\) makes the partition function factorize:
\[
Z=\prod_\mu(1+e^{-\lambda_\mu}),\qquad
n_\mu=\frac{1}{1+e^{\lambda_\mu}},\qquad
\lambda_\mu=\ln\frac{1-n_\mu}{n_\mu}.
\tag{11.2}\]
Exactly empty or full modes are allowed as limits \(\lambda_\mu\to\pm\infty\). A conventional thermal state is the special case \(\lambda_\mu=\beta(\epsilon_\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{chem}})\). A general quench produces an independent function of mode label instead.
The real-space covariance follows directly:
\[
C_{ij}(t)\equiv\ev{c_i^\dagger(t)c_j(t)}
=\sum_{\mu\nu}\phi_\mu^*(i)\phi_\nu(j)
e^{i(\epsilon_\mu-\epsilon_\nu)t}\ev{d_\mu^\dagger d_\nu}_0.
\tag{11.3}\]
For nondegenerate one-particle energies its infinite-time average retains only \(\mu=\nu\), exactly as predicted by the occupation GGE. In an extended system many frequencies dephase and local instantaneous correlations can settle near this value. A finite system remains quasiperiodic and can recur. Statements about stationary local states usually take the thermodynamic limit before the long-time limit.
Degeneracies require care: if \(\epsilon_\mu=\epsilon_\nu\), the coherence \(d_\mu^\dagger d_\nu\) is conserved too. One can diagonalize the initial covariance within each degenerate subspace, or constrain the entire stationary covariance block. Occupations in an arbitrary basis need not suffice. Pairing Hamiltonians similarly require a Nambu covariance containing both \(\ev{c_i^\dagger c_j}\) and \(\ev{c_i c_j}\).
For a Gaussian state, Wick’s rule expresses every even correlation as sums of products of two-point functions. For example,
\[
\ev{c_i^\dagger c_j^\dagger c_l c_m}
=C_{im}C_{jl}-C_{il}C_{jm}
\]
when anomalous correlations vanish. Quadratic evolution preserves Gaussianity. For initially non-Gaussian states, using Wick’s rule needs an additional argument: spreading particles can dilute connected higher-order correlations in a fixed observation region. Rigorous forms of this gaussification require assumptions such as clustering in the initial state and delocalizing one-particle propagation  [2]. Localized modes, insufficient transport, persistent degeneracies, and long-range initial correlations can obstruct the argument.
The global diagonal ensemble can retain correlations \(\ev{I_\mu I_\nu}_0-n_\mu n_\nu\) that Equation 11.2 discards. A GGE may nevertheless reproduce every fixed-support observable because the contribution of that information becomes negligible locally. Equality of local states is much weaker than equality of global density operators or entropies.






TipSolved example: density-wave melting



Take \(H=-J\sum_j(c_j^\dagger c_{j+1}+\mathrm{h.c.})\) on an even periodic chain and initially occupy every even site. Each momentum mode has \(n_k=1/2\), so its occupation GGE is the infinite-temperature state at half filling. The initial state also has \(\ev{c_k^\dagger c_{k+\pi}}=1/2\) with a sign fixed by the origin convention. Since \(\epsilon_k=-2J\cos k\), the staggered density becomes, in the infinite chain,
\[
m(t)\equiv\frac1L\sum_j(-1)^j\ev{n_j(t)}
=\frac12\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{\dd k}{2\pi}e^{-4iJt\cos k}
=\frac12 J_0(4Jt).
\]
Here \(J_0\) is defined by the displayed integral. Its oscillatory envelope decays as \(t^{-1/2}\). The occupations never change; relaxation comes from the off-diagonal momentum coherence.

title: 11  Integrability and constrained equilibrium
section: 11.3 Hard-core bosons and the Jordan–Wigner string
text:
11.3 Hard-core bosons and the Jordan–Wigner string
Hard-core bosons obey \(b_j^2=0\) and \(\{b_j,b_j^\dagger\}=1\) on one site, while operators on different sites commute. In an open chain define
\[
b_j=\exp\left(i\pi\sum_{l<j}c_l^\dagger c_l\right)c_j,
\qquad n_j=b_j^\dagger b_j=c_j^\dagger c_j.
\tag{11.4}\]
The string supplies the minus signs needed to turn fermionic exchange into bosonic exchange. Nearest-neighbor hopping maps to fermion hopping, so the many-body energies and density dynamics are free-fermionic. On a ring the boundary hopping depends on fermion parity; calculations must select the appropriate parity sector and boundary condition.
Off-diagonal bosonic correlations contain strings. For \(i<j\),
\[
\ev{b_i^\dagger b_j}
=\left\langle c_i^\dagger
\prod_{i<l<j}(1-2n_l)c_j\right\rangle.
\tag{11.5}\]
These can be evaluated by expanding the product and applying Wick’s rule, or more efficiently as determinants/Pfaffians of a covariance matrix. At separation two, Wick’s rule gives the explicit check
\[
\ev{b_i^\dagger b_{i+2}}
=C_{i,i+2}(1-2C_{i+1,i+1})
+2C_{i,i+1}C_{i+1,i+2}.
\]
Thus bosonic momentum occupations, obtained by Fourier transforming Equation 11.5, can change substantially although fermionic mode occupations are constants. The mapping changes the form of the observable. For fixed \(j-i\), the string has finite support; local fermionic gaussification can then determine its late-time value. A momentum distribution sums all separations, so interchange of the long-distance, thermodynamic, and long-time limits needs further control.

title: 11  Integrability and constrained equilibrium
text:
11.4 Generalized eigenstate thermalization
Ordinary ETH says that energy density determines local properties of a typical chaotic eigenstate. Integrable eigenstates at the same energy can have different mode distributions and different local observables. The replacement is a macrostate containing all relevant conserved densities. Eigenstates that represent the same smooth macrostate should become locally indistinguishable as \(L\) grows. This is the useful content of generalized ETH, rather than a claim that all same-energy integrable eigenstates agree  [3].
For free particles this is transparent. A momentum-occupation eigenstate has
\[
\ev{c_j^\dagger c_{j+r}}=\frac1L\sum_k e^{ikr}n_k.
\]
Divide momentum space into bins of width \(\Delta k\) with \(L^{-1}\ll\Delta k\ll1\). If two eigenstates have the same occupied fraction in each bin, the difference of their fixed-\(r\) correlations vanishes as the bin width shrinks. Within a bin, \(e^{ikr}\) barely changes. Wick’s rule extends the result to finite-support fermionic observables. There remain exponentially many microscopic occupation patterns compatible with each smooth distribution. A generalized microcanonical ensemble samples these patterns; a GGE assigns Lagrange multipliers to their macroscopic constraints. Their local equivalence is an ensemble-equivalence statement with regularity assumptions, not an identity at finite size.

title: 11  Integrability and constrained equilibrium
text:
11.5 A transverse-field Ising quench
Consider
\[
H(h)=-J\sum_j\left(\sigma_j^x\sigma_{j+1}^x+h\sigma_j^z\right),
\qquad J>0.
\]
With \(\sigma_j^z=1-2c_j^\dagger c_j\), a Jordan–Wigner transformation turns the spin interaction into hopping plus pairing. Fourier transformation groups modes \(k,-k\). Diagonalizing their \(2\times2\) particle-hole matrix is a rotation with angle
\[
e^{i\theta_k(h)}=\frac{h-\cos k+i\sin k}{\sqrt{1+h^2-2h\cos k}},
\qquad \epsilon_k(h)=2J\sqrt{1+h^2-2h\cos k}.
\tag{11.6}\]
The resulting Bogoliubov operators satisfy \(H=\sum_k\epsilon_k(\gamma_k^\dagger\gamma_k-1/2)\). If the initial state is the ground state at \(h_0\) and time evolution uses \(h\), composing the two rotations gives, up to an irrelevant pair phase,
\[
\ket{\psi_0}=\prod_{k>0}\left[
\cos\frac{\Delta\theta_k}{2}
+i\sin\frac{\Delta\theta_k}{2}\gamma_k^\dagger\gamma_{-k}^\dagger
\right]\ket{0_h},\quad
\Delta\theta_k=\theta_k(h)-\theta_k(h_0).
\]
Consequently
\[
n_k=\ev{\gamma_k^\dagger\gamma_k}_0
=\sin^2\frac{\Delta\theta_k}{2}
=\frac{1-\cos\Delta\theta_k}{2}.
\tag{11.7}\]
At each positive \(k\), the state is a superposition of an empty and a doubly occupied pair. Its diagonal ensemble therefore has \(\ev{I_k I_{-k}}=n_k\), whereas a product occupation GGE gives \(n_k^2\). This illustrates the global/local distinction concretely. Oscillating anomalous terms have frequencies \(2\epsilon_k\) and disappear from generic fixed-support late-time correlations when dispersive dephasing applies.
For example, the stationary transverse magnetization is
\[
\ev{\sigma^z}_{\mathrm{stat}}
=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{\dd k}{2\pi}
\cos\theta_k(h)\,[1-2n_k].
\]
For a quench from \(h_0\to+\infty\) to \(h=1\), \(\theta_k(h_0)=0\) and \(\cos\theta_k(1)=\abs{\sin(k/2)}\). The integral is the average of \(\sin^2(k/2)\), hence \(\ev{\sigma^z}_{\mathrm{stat}}=1/2\). This calculation uses a covariance integral instead of a sum over \(2^L\) spin states. At flat-dispersion points, such as \(h=0\), persistent coherent oscillations need separate treatment.

11.5.1 Truncating the charges
Mode occupations are nonlocal, but suitable combinations are local. In the Ising chain, multiplying the quadratic Hamiltonian’s momentum-space matrix by \(\cos(rk)\) creates a conserved quadratic charge with support extending only a distance of order \(r\). Its Bogoliubov form is proportional to \(\sum_k\epsilon_k\cos(rk)(I_k-1/2)\). Current-type charges supply the appropriate odd-in-\(k\) family when the state requires it. Taking sufficiently many such charges is equivalent, for regular translation-invariant states, to specifying the mode distribution.
A truncated GGE retains only charges with range up to a cutoff \(R\), chooses their multipliers from the initial expectations, and predicts a finite subsystem density matrix. Increasing \(R\) restores increasingly detailed spatial information. The practical target is convergence of the reduced state or of selected correlations as \(R\) grows. It is not exact recovery of every \(n_k\) at a small cutoff. Studies of the Ising chain show why the shortest-range charges are especially valuable for small subsystems  [4]. Near criticality or for nonsmooth mode data, convergence can be slower; there is no universal finite cutoff that works for all states and observables.

title: 11  Integrability and constrained equilibrium
section: 11.6 Interacting integrability: the XXZ completeness problem
text:
11.6 Interacting integrability: the XXZ completeness problem
The spin-\(1/2\) XXZ chain,
\[
H=J\sum_j\left(S_j^xS_{j+1}^x+S_j^yS_{j+1}^y
+\Delta S_j^zS_{j+1}^z\right),\qquad S^a=\sigma^a/2,
\]
is interacting after fermionization. In the gapped regime \(\Delta=\cosh\eta>1\), its Bethe quasiparticles include bound complexes of \(a=1,2,\ldots\) overturned spins. A homogeneous thermodynamic eigenstate is described by particle and hole densities \(\rho_a(\lambda)\) and \(\rho_a^h(\lambda)\) for each species, with rapidity \(\lambda\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\). Rapidity plays the role of a momentum parameter. Scattering changes the available density of states, giving coupled constraints
\[
\rho_a+\rho_a^h=a_a-\sum_b K_{ab}*\rho_b,
\qquad
a_a(\lambda)=\frac{\sinh(a\eta)}{\pi[\cosh(a\eta)-\cos(2\lambda)]}.
\tag{11.8}\]
Here \(*\) integrates over the rapidity interval. One standard kernel convention is \(K_{ab}=(1-\delta_{ab})a_{|a-b|}+2\sum_{j=1}^{\min(a,b)-1}a_{|a-b|+2j}+a_{a+b}\). This equation is the interacting counterpart of counting allowed free momentum states. A charge density has the linear form \(q_\alpha=\sum_a\int\dd\lambda\,q_{\alpha a}(\lambda)\rho_a(\lambda)\). Its one-particle eigenvalues \(q_{\alpha a}\) characterize which species and rapidities that charge can distinguish.
Counting ways to fill particle/hole slots gives the entropy density
\[
s_{\mathrm{YY}}=\sum_a\int\dd\lambda\,
\left[(\rho_a+\rho_a^h)\ln(\rho_a+\rho_a^h)
-\rho_a\ln\rho_a-\rho_a^h\ln\rho_a^h\right].
\]
Maximizing it subject to Equation 11.8 and the charges is a generalized thermodynamic Bethe ansatz. It reduces the stationary-state problem to functions of one variable, but only if the constraints determine the root densities. An infinite list of charges can still be incomplete: infinitely many measurements of one combination need not distinguish all bound-state species.
This issue became decisive in quenches from the Néel product state \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow\cdots}\) (or its translation-symmetric combination). A GGE using the then-standard strictly local transfer-matrix charges disagreed with an independently obtained quench-action stationary state  [5]. The quench-action method weights thermodynamic eigenstates by their overlaps with the initial state and their state-counting entropy, then finds the dominant macrostate. It provides a useful independent benchmark rather than assuming a chosen charge list is complete.
The resolution was to include additional quasilocal charges: extensive operators whose density has spatial tails that decay sufficiently fast, rather than stopping at a fixed range. Suitable families distinguish information about bound quasiparticle densities missed by the earlier charge set, and a complete construction recovers the tested stationary state  [6]. Thus the failure of a particular GGE is a diagnosis of missing constraints, not a disproof of maximum entropy. The explicit kernels and charge families depend on the anisotropy regime; the formulas above were restricted to \(\Delta>1\) for that reason.

title: 11  Integrability and constrained equilibrium
text:
11.7 Exercises and worked answers

Same energy, different equilibrium. For three free modes with energies \((-1,0,1)\), compare occupation profiles \((1/2,0,1/2)\) and \((0,1,0)\). Do particle number and energy determine the GGE?
Answer. Both have \(N=1\) and \(E=0\), but their central occupations are 0 and 1. A measurement of \(I_2\) distinguishes them. Two constraints cannot determine three independent occupation expectations. Thermalization requires a mechanism that changes the extra conserved data.
A global distinction. A pair of modes has the diagonal state \(\rho=(1-n)\ket{00}\bra{00}+n\ket{11}\bra{11}\). Compute its entropy and that of the product GGE with the same occupations.
Answer. Write \(h(n)=-n\ln n-(1-n)\ln(1-n)\). The diagonal state has entropy \(h(n)\); the product state has entropy \(2h(n)\). The missing \(h(n)\) is their classical mutual information. Local equivalence in a many-mode spatial limit does not imply equal extensive entropies.
Check a bosonic string. Expand \(\ev{b_i^\dagger b_{i+2}}\) and derive the expression in this chapter using Wick’s rule.
Answer. The string is \(1-2n_{i+1}\). Wick’s rule gives \(\ev{c_i^\dagger n_{i+1}c_{i+2}}=C_{i,i+2}C_{i+1,i+1}-C_{i,i+1}C_{i+1,i+2}\). Subtract twice this from \(C_{i,i+2}\).
Design a completeness test. What would demonstrate that a charge set is insufficient even if it contains infinitely many members?
Answer. Find two admissible macrostates with identical values of all listed charges and different values of a local observable. Equivalently, find a nonzero change \(\delta\rho_a\) satisfying the linearized Bethe constraints and \(\sum_a\int q_{\alpha a}\delta\rho_a=0\) for every listed \(\alpha\), while changing a physical correlation. Counting charges alone cannot exclude such a null space.
