[2] M. Gluza, C. Krumnow, M. Friesdorf, C. Gogolin, and J. Eisert, Equilibration via gaussification in fermionic lattice systems, Physical Review Letters 117, 190602 (2016).


[3] A. C. Cassidy, C. W. Clark, and M. Rigol, Generalized thermalization in an integrable lattice system, Physical Review Letters 106, 140405 (2011).


[4] M. Fagotti and F. H. L. Essler, Reduced density matrix after a quantum quench, Physical Review B 87, 245107 (2013).


[5] B. Wouters, J. De Nardis, M. Brockmann, D. Fioretto, M. Rigol, and J.-S. Caux, Quenching the anisotropic heisenberg chain: Exact solution and generalized gibbs ensemble predictions, Physical Review Letters 113, 117202 (2014).


[6] E. Ilievski, J. De Nardis, B. Wouters, J.-S. Caux, F. H. L. Essler, and T. Prosen, Complete generalized gibbs ensembles in an interacting theory, Physical Review Letters 115, 157201 (2015).

title: 12  Prethermalization and kinetic relaxation
text:
12.1 Fast relaxation and slowly changing charges
A small violation of integrability need not immediately erase the conserved information described in the previous chapter. Local correlations can relax rapidly to a constrained state, remain near it for a long interval, and only later move toward thermal equilibrium. This separation of stages is called prethermalization. It is a statement about a hierarchy of dynamical time scales, not a new exact equilibrium ensemble.
This chapter derives a useful weak-coupling description. We distinguish exact perturbative identities from the assumptions that turn them into irreversible kinetic equations. Throughout, \(\hbar=k_B=1\).
Write
\[
H=H_0+gV,\qquad [H_0,Q_\alpha]=0,
\tag{12.1}\]
where \(g\) is dimensionless and small, and \(V\) has the dimensions of energy. The exact equation is \(\dd\ev{Q_\alpha}/\dd t=ig\ev{[V,Q_\alpha]}\). If dephasing under \(H_0\) produces a locally stationary GGE on a time \(\tau_{\mathrm{deph}}\), we may hope that, at later times, the state is approximately specified by slowly varying expectations \(q_\alpha(t)\). The proposed local description is
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{slow}}(t)=Z(t)^{-1}
\exp\left[-\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha(t)Q_\alpha\right].
\]
This ansatz concerns finite-support observables; the exact global state remains unitarily related to the initial state. If it is diagonal in a common charge basis, \(\tr\rho_{\mathrm{slow}}[V,Q_\alpha]=0\). Indeed, the diagonal matrix elements of that commutator vanish. Dissipative charge drift then usually starts at order \(g^2\), while order-\(g\) effects can renormalize energies or generate coherent motion within degenerate subspaces.
An observed plateau may therefore correspond to a GGE of dressed approximate charges, rather than the bare \(Q_\alpha\). Weak interaction quenches in fermionic systems give concrete examples of correlation buildup, a long-lived nonthermal distribution, and later kinetic relaxation  [1]. Detailed numerical work also finds prethermal plateaux and their subsequent drift in models with weak integrability breaking  [2]. These are model-dependent observations supporting the framework, not a guarantee for every perturbation.

title: 12  Prethermalization and kinetic relaxation
section: 12.2 What second-order perturbation theory actually gives
text:
12.2 What second-order perturbation theory actually gives
In the interaction picture, \(V_I(t)=e^{iH_0t}Ve^{-iH_0t}\) and \(\dot\rho_I=-ig[V_I(t),\rho_I]\). Integrating once and substituting back into the expectation-value equation gives
\[
\frac{\dd\ev{Q_\alpha}}{\dd t}
=ig\tr\rho_0[V_I(t),Q_\alpha]
-g^2\int_0^t\dd s\,
\tr\rho_0[V_I(s),[V_I(t),Q_\alpha]]+O(g^3)
\tag{12.2}\]
at fixed time. This expression contains memory of the preparation. It is not yet a closed equation for \(q_\alpha(t)\), and its error estimate is not uniform at arbitrarily long times. Terms proportional to \(g^2t\) eventually invalidate a naive fixed-order expansion.
To obtain a kinetic equation one assumes that the correlation kernel decays on a time \(\tau_c\), while the occupations change on a much longer time \(\tau_{\mathrm{kin}}\). One then replaces the old state inside the kernel by the slowly evolving local GGE, neglects its change during \(\tau_c\), and extends the memory integral to infinity. This is a Markov approximation with a separation of time scales. Taking \(g\to0\) while \(g^2t\) stays finite identifies the usual kinetic limit.
The real part of the oscillatory integral selects resonant transitions. For two eigenstates of \(H_0\), first-order transition amplitudes give
\[
P_{a\leftarrow b}(t)
=g^2\abs{V_{ab}}^2
\frac{4\sin^2[(E_a-E_b)t/2]}{(E_a-E_b)^2}.
\]
In a dense spectrum, integrated against a smooth function of energy, \(4\sin^2(\omega t/2)/(t\omega^2)\to2\pi\delta(\omega)\). Therefore the transition rate is
\[
W_{a\leftarrow b}=2\pi g^2\abs{V_{ab}}^2\delta(E_a-E_b).
\tag{12.3}\]
Principal-value contributions from the imaginary part shift energies and should be absorbed into the effective quasiparticle dynamics when relevant. A finite isolated system has discrete lines, so replacing the sinc peak by a delta function requires an intermediate time window: long compared with microscopic correlation times, short enough that individual level discreteness and recurrences do not dominate. The thermodynamic and weak-coupling limits are part of the argument.
For a Hermitian static perturbation the leading rates are symmetric under \(a\leftrightarrow b\). An approximate master equation has \(\dot p_a=\sum_b(W_{a\leftarrow b}p_b-W_{b\leftarrow a}p_a)\). It preserves probability and redistributes weight among resonant states. Its apparent irreversibility comes from discarding coherences and memory, not from modifying the exact unitary law.

title: 12  Prethermalization and kinetic relaxation
section: 12.3 From many-body transitions to a fermionic collision integral
text:
12.3 From many-body transitions to a fermionic collision integral
For weakly interacting fermions take \(H_0=\sum_k\epsilon_k n_k\). A two-body interaction contains terms \(c_1^\dagger c_2^\dagger c_4c_3\). The indices include momentum and any spin or band label. A collision transfers two occupied incoming modes to two empty outgoing modes. If the local state approximately factorizes in quasiparticle occupations, its probability contains products of \(n_k\) and \(1-n_k\).
With a nonnegative rate \(\mathcal W_{12;34}\) that includes the golden-rule factor, the momentum and energy constraints, the antisymmetrized matrix element, and consistent counting of equivalent channels, one obtains
\[
\dot n_1=\sum_{234}\mathcal W_{12;34}
\left[(1-n_1)(1-n_2)n_3n_4
-n_1n_2(1-n_3)(1-n_4)\right].
\tag{12.4}\]
We use the ordered-index convention in which the rate is symmetric under \(1\leftrightarrow2\), \(3\leftrightarrow4\), and \((12)\leftrightarrow(34)\); any identical-particle counting factor belongs in \(\mathcal W\). The two terms are gain and loss. Pauli blocking is essential: a collision cannot fill an already occupied fermion mode. Bosonic collisions instead contain stimulated-emission factors \(1+n\).
The energy constraint is \(\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3+\epsilon_4\). Crystal momentum is conserved modulo a reciprocal lattice vector. Summing Equation 12.4 over all modes and pairing gain with loss proves \(\dot N=0\). Multiplication by \(\epsilon_1\) and symmetrization proves conservation of \(\sum_k\epsilon_kn_k\). This is the leading kinetic energy; conservation of the exact interacting energy may require quasiparticle shifts and correlation-energy corrections at higher order.
The closure assumes that correlations between incoming occupations can be neglected at the accuracy of interest. It can fail during initial correlation buildup, near singular resonances, or when additional slow variables are omitted. Integrable interacting quasiparticles require their own scattering and charge structure; a bare free-particle equation should not be transplanted without a derivation.

title: 12  Prethermalization and kinetic relaxation
section: 12.4 An entropy theorem and the destination of collisions
text:
12.4 An entropy theorem and the destination of collisions
Define the fermionic kinetic entropy
\[
S_{\mathrm{kin}}=-\sum_k[n_k\ln n_k+(1-n_k)\ln(1-n_k)].
\]
It is the entropy of a product occupation ensemble, not the conserved entropy of the exact isolated density matrix. Put \(X=(1-n_1)(1-n_2)n_3n_4\) and \(Y=n_1n_2(1-n_3)(1-n_4)\). Differentiating and using the rate symmetries gives
\[
\dot S_{\mathrm{kin}}=
\frac14\sum_{1234}\mathcal W_{12;34}(X-Y)\ln\frac XY\geq0.
\tag{12.5}\]
The inequality follows because \(\ln x\) is increasing. If \(X>Y\), both factors are positive; if \(X<Y\), both are negative. Zero occupations are handled by continuous limits. The factor \(1/4\) comes from averaging over exchanging the two members of each pair and exchanging incoming with outgoing states.
Equality requires \(X=Y\) for every active channel. Let \(\varphi_k=\ln[n_k/(1-n_k)]\). The stationarity condition is
\[
\varphi_1+\varphi_2=\varphi_3+\varphi_4
\]
on all allowed collisions. Thus every additive collision invariant produces a stationary distribution. If particle number and energy are the only independent invariants and the collision network connects the relevant states, then
\[
\varphi_k=\beta\mu-\beta\epsilon_k,\qquad
n_k=\frac{1}{e^{\beta(\epsilon_k-\mu)}+1}.
\]
If ordinary momentum is conserved without Umklapp processes, a drifting distribution can include a term proportional to momentum. If channels are disconnected, additional invariants survive and a nonthermal stationary state is possible. The entropy theorem proves monotonicity within the kinetic approximation; convergence to a unique thermal state needs these extra connectivity assumptions.






NoteA one-dimensional kinematic obstruction



For identical particles with \(\epsilon_k=k^2/(2m)\), two-body collisions conserve \(P=k_1+k_2\) and \(k_1^2+k_2^2\). Since \(k_1k_2=[P^2-(k_1^2+k_2^2)]/2\), the outgoing momenta solve the same quadratic equation as the incoming ones. Hence \(\{k_3,k_4\}=\{k_1,k_2\}\). Such collisions only exchange labels and cannot relax the distribution. Thermalization then needs another channel: three-body scattering, a lattice dispersion with suitable phase space, additional species, or another integrability-breaking process. A formal \(g^2\) prefactor does not establish a nonzero relaxation rate.

title: 12  Prethermalization and kinetic relaxation
section: 12.5 Time scales and the interpretation of a plateau
text:
12.5 Time scales and the interpretation of a plateau
If a typical resonant rate is \(g^2J\) for microscopic energy \(J\), dimensional analysis suggests \(\tau_{\mathrm{kin}}\sim(g^2J)^{-1}\). The prethermal window is \(\tau_{\mathrm{deph}}\ll t\ll\tau_{\mathrm{kin}}\). This estimate assumes nonvanishing second-order phase space and nonsingular matrix elements. Selection rules can eliminate the leading channel. Low-temperature Pauli blocking can add strong temperature factors. Approximate symmetries, constrained dynamics, and higher-order processes can produce other powers or much longer times. High-frequency driven prethermalization is another mechanism and need not obey this weak-static-perturbation estimate.
A useful numerical diagnosis follows several observables. First establish fast decay of oscillations. Then test whether intermediate values agree with an appropriate GGE or dressed-charge ensemble. Finally vary \(g\) and check a predicted rescaling of the slow drift, while controlling finite size and accessible time. A flat trace by itself cannot distinguish a true stationary state from an unresolved slow evolution.
The hierarchy also clarifies what “thermalization” means operationally. A system may have nearly thermal densities while its momentum distribution is still nonthermal, or short-range correlators may settle while a transport mode relaxes slowly. The chosen observables and tolerance belong in any quoted equilibration time.

title: 12  Prethermalization and kinetic relaxation
text:
12.6 Exercises and worked answers

Verify charge conservation. Show directly that Equation 12.4 conserves a quantity \(Q_f=\sum_k f_kn_k\) whenever \(f_1+f_2=f_3+f_4\) for every active collision.
Answer. After the same symmetrization used in the entropy proof, \(\dot Q_f=\tfrac14\sum\mathcal W(X-Y)(f_1+f_2-f_3-f_4)=0\). Choosing \(f=1\) and \(f=\epsilon\) gives number and energy.
A single reaction channel. Consider four distinct modes with only \(12\leftrightarrow34\) allowed. Why need its stationary state not be determined by number and energy alone?
Answer. Each event changes occupations by a multiple of \((-1,-1,+1,+1)\). Every vector \(f\) orthogonal to this vector is invariant, a three-dimensional space. For example \(n_1-n_2\) and \(n_3-n_4\) are separately conserved. Detailed balance fixes only one relation among four occupations. More channels are needed for thermal uniqueness.
Scaling test. Suppose the same local observable obeys \(A(t)-A_{\mathrm{th}}\simeq A_0e^{-cg^2Jt}\). What happens when \(g\) is halved?
Answer. The slow decay time increases by four. Curves should approximately collapse when plotted against \(g^2Jt\) after the initial transient. Failure of collapse can indicate higher-order processes, a changed plateau, finite-size effects, or the absence of the assumed kinetic regime; it is not by itself evidence against unitary dynamics.
Entropy accounting. How can Equation 12.5 coexist with constant exact von Neumann entropy?
Answer. \(S_{\mathrm{kin}}\) uses only single-mode occupations and discards intermode correlations. Unitary evolution can move information into correlations while the entropy of the maximum-entropy product state consistent with the retained data rises. The two entropies are functions of different information.





[1] M. Moeckel and S. Kehrein, Interaction quench in the hubbard model, Physical Review Letters 100, 175702 (2008).


[2] B. Bertini, F. H. L. Essler, S. Groha, and N. J. Robinson, Prethermalization and thermalization in models with weak integrability breaking, Physical Review Letters 115, 180601 (2015).

title: 13  Mathematical tools and two revealing examples
text:
13.1 The kicked rotor: from a map to localization
This chapter collects the seven auxiliary topics behind the book’s main argument. The kicked rotor illustrates the distinction between classical diffusion and quantum interference. Zeta zeros illustrate spectral universality and the limits of numerical evidence. The remaining sections provide proofs and continuum derivations that can be reused independently. A probability vector is a column vector throughout; a doubly stochastic matrix has both row sums and column sums equal to one.
crumbs: 13  Mathematical tools and two revealing examples

title: 13  Mathematical tools and two revealing examples
text:
13.1.1 Classical stroboscopic dynamics
Choose dimensionless time with one kick per unit interval and Hamiltonian
\[
H(\theta,P,t)=\frac{P^2}{2}+K\cos\theta\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\delta(t-n),
\qquad \theta\equiv\theta+2\pi.
\]
Let \((\theta_n,P_n)\) denote the state just before kick \(n\). Integrating Hamilton’s equation through the impulse and then through free rotation gives the standard map:
\[
P_{n+1}=P_n+K\sin\theta_n,\qquad
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+P_{n+1}\pmod{2\pi}.
\tag{13.1}\]
Its tangent matrix in the order \((\theta,P)\) is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1+K\cos\theta&1\\K\cos\theta&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), with determinant one. Thus phase-space area is preserved even when nearby trajectories separate exponentially. For small kicks many invariant curves survive; for stronger kicks large chaotic regions appear, with regular islands often remaining.
The fixed points at \(P=0\) are \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=\pi\). Their tangent eigenvalues obey
\[
\lambda^2-(2+K\cos\theta_*)\lambda+1=0.
\]
For our positive-cosine kick convention, \(\theta_*=\pi\) is the potential minimum. Its trace is \(2-K\), so for \(0<K<4\) the eigenvalues are a complex-conjugate pair of modulus one: the fixed point is elliptic at linear order. At \(K>4\) they become real reciprocal eigenvalues, one with modulus larger than one, giving a hyperbolic instability. At \(\theta_*=0\), the trace is \(2+K>2\), so that point is hyperbolic for every \(K>0\). The endpoints \(K=0,4\) are marginal and need nonlinear analysis. Near the elliptic point, writing \(\theta=\pi+q\) gives \(q_{n+1}-2q_n+q_{n-1}\simeq-Kq_n\); for \(K\ll1\) this approaches a pendulum’s small-oscillation equation. Hyperbolicity of a fixed point is local information: it does not prove that the entire map is chaotic or determine the threshold for unrestricted momentum transport.
If successive angles were independent and uniform, each momentum increment would have mean zero and variance \(K^2/2\). Then \(\ev{(P_n-P_0)^2}\simeq D_Pn\), with \(D_P\simeq K^2/2\). This random-phase estimate is useful in a strongly chaotic regime. Correlations between kicks, trapping near islands, and accelerator modes can change the diffusion coefficient or even the diffusion law. Classical chaos alone does not justify treating every kick as independent noise.


13.1.2 Floquet evolution
Quantization gives momentum states \(\ket m\) with \(P\ket m=\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}m\ket m\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\). Wavefunctions are periodic in \(\theta\); equivalently, \([\theta,P]=i\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}\) holds in the usual local angular-coordinate sense. Evolution from just before one kick to just before the next is
\[
U_F=\exp\left(-\frac{iP^2}{2\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right)
\exp\left(-\frac{iK\cos\theta}{\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right).
\tag{13.2}\]
Using the Fourier expansion \(e^{-iz\cos\theta}=\sum_l(-i)^lJ_l(z)e^{il\theta}\) gives
\[
\bra{m}U_F\ket{n}
=e^{-i\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}m^2/2}
(-i)^{m-n}J_{m-n}(K/\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}).
\]
A numerical simulation can alternate a diagonal kick in angle representation with a diagonal free phase in momentum representation, using Fourier transforms. A momentum cutoff must be large enough that the spreading wavepacket never reaches its artificial boundary.
For generic nonresonant parameters in a classically diffusive regime, interference can stop the quantum momentum spreading. Floquet eigenstates become localized in momentum, with envelopes schematically \(\abs{\psi_m}^2\sim e^{-2|m-m_0|/\ell}\). The relation between the rotor eigenvalue problem and a one-dimensional Anderson-type lattice problem explains this dynamical localization  [1]. The phase sequence is deterministic, so one must not silently replace every parameter choice by independent random disorder.
A useful scaling estimate compares classical spreading in mode number, \(\ev{(\Delta m)^2}\sim(D_P/\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}^2)n\), with a break time of order the number \(\ell\) of appreciably occupied Floquet components. Setting \(\ell^2\sim(D_P/\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}^2)\ell\) gives \(\ell\sim D_P/\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}^2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{break}}\sim\ell\), up to convention-dependent numerical factors. This is a scaling argument, not an exact formula across all \(K\).
Resonances are an essential exception. When \(\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}/(4\pi)\) is rational, the free phases are periodic in momentum and resonance or antiresonance may replace localization. For \(\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}=4\pi\), the free operator is the identity. Starting from \(m=0\), after \(n\) kicks the angle wavefunction is proportional to \(e^{-inK\cos\theta/\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}}\), so \(\ev{P^2}=K^2n^2/2\): ballistic growth. At \(\hbar_{\mathrm{eff}}=2\pi\), the free evolution translates the angle by \(\pi\), successive cosine kicks cancel, and \(U_F^2=1\). For a kicked particle rather than a rotor, conserved quasimomentum introduces another resonance condition. Weak noise or decoherence can also destroy interference and restore long-time diffusion.

section: 13.2 Zeta zeros: unfolding, evidence, and conjecture
text:
13.2 Zeta zeros: unfolding, evidence, and conjecture
For \(\Re s>1\), the Riemann zeta function is \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\geq1}n^{-s}\). Analytic continuation defines it elsewhere, apart from its pole at \(s=1\). Its nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip \(0<\Re s<1\). The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all lie on \(\Re s=1/2\). It is separate from statements about spacing correlations.
Write zeros on the critical line as \(1/2+i\gamma_n\) with positive increasing \(\gamma_n\). In a range in which all zeros are known to lie on that line, or conditionally on the Riemann hypothesis, a smooth counting function is
\[
\overline N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\ln\frac{T}{2\pi}
-\frac{T}{2\pi}+\frac78.
\]
The local density changes slowly with height: \(\overline N'(T)=(2\pi)^{-1}\ln(T/2\pi)\). Raw spacings at different heights are therefore incomparable. Define unfolded positions \(x_n=\overline N(\gamma_n)\) and spacings \(s_n=x_{n+1}-x_n\). Their local mean approaches one. In a narrow window near \(T\), the equivalent approximation is \(s_n\simeq(\gamma_{n+1}-\gamma_n)\ln(T/2\pi)/(2\pi)\).
The conjectured distinct-pair correlation is the bulk GUE expression
\[
R_2(s)=1-\left(\frac{\sin\pi s}{\pi s}\right)^2.
\tag{13.3}\]
The self-pair delta function at \(s=0\) is excluded from this convention. Expanding the sine shows \(R_2(s)\sim\pi^2s^2/3\) near zero, a form of quadratic repulsion. Pair correlation is not the same statistic as the nearest-neighbor distribution, although both can be compared with random matrices.
Montgomery obtained conditional results for a restricted Fourier range and proposed the fuller pair-correlation statement  [2]. Odlyzko’s high-precision computations found detailed numerical agreement with random-matrix predictions  [3]. This is strong numerical evidence for spectral universality. It is neither a proof of the full correlation conjecture nor a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
The Hilbert–Pólya idea asks whether a suitable self-adjoint operator could encode the zeros as spectral data, so that its real eigenvalues would force their real parts to be \(1/2\). A successful proof needs a rigorously established correspondence with all relevant zeros; merely constructing an operator with selected imaginary parts as eigenvalues achieves nothing by itself. No such operator or proof is supplied by matching a spacing histogram. The physics lesson is methodological: a universal statistic can reveal structure without identifying its microscopic mechanism.

13.2.1 Prime modes and complex-temperature zeros
Unique prime factorization supplies another connection to statistical mechanics. For \(\Re s>1\), absolute convergence permits expanding
\[
\prod_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}
=\prod_p\sum_{n_p\geq0}p^{-sn_p}
=\sum_{n\geq1}n^{-s}=\zeta(s).
\]
Each choice of nonnegative integers \(n_p\) corresponds to exactly one integer \(n=\prod_pp^{n_p}\). Introduce independent bosonic modes with normal-ordered energies \(H=E_*\sum_p(\ln p)N_p\), where \(E_*>0\) sets the energy unit and the vacuum energy is zero. A Fock state then has energy \(E_n=E_*\ln n\), with one state per positive integer. Its partition function is
\[
Z(\beta)=\prod_p\frac1{1-e^{-\beta E_*\ln p}}
=\zeta(\beta E_*),\qquad \Re(\beta E_*)>1.
\]
The convergence restriction is physical: at high enough temperature the increasing number of accessible logarithmic-energy levels makes the trace diverge. Analytically continuing \(\zeta\) beyond this domain does not make that divergent trace a thermal state. In particular, the critical-line zeros are outside the domain of this literal infinite-mode Gibbs ensemble. This distinction prevents the partition-function analogy from becoming a purported physical proof about the zeros.
For any Hamiltonian with a convergent Gibbs trace, its energy probability distribution has characteristic function
\[
\chi_\beta(u)=\ev{e^{iuH}}_\beta
=\frac{Z(\beta-iu)}{Z(\beta)}.
\]
Here \(u\) has units of inverse energy. Thus zeros of the characteristic function are complex-temperature zeros of the partition function on the corresponding vertical line. Zeros in complex inverse temperature are called Fisher zeros. A finite-level cutoff makes \(Z\) a finite sum, so its complex zeros are unambiguous; interpreting their accumulation as a thermodynamic singularity requires a specified limit. Neither analytic continuation nor removal of a cutoff can be interchanged with that limit without justification. For the untruncated prime-mode model, the Euler product has no zeros in its convergent half-plane, so its physical characteristic function does not sample the critical-line zeros.
A related Loschmidt amplitude is obtained by purifying the Gibbs state: \(\ket{\Psi_\beta}=\sum_n\sqrt{p_n}\ket n\ket n\). Evolving only one copy gives overlap \(Z(\beta+it/\hbar)/Z(\beta)\). This establishes a precise relation to return amplitudes for that preparation, not for an arbitrary quench. Proposed broader links between complex-zero patterns and ergodicity remain conjectural. The prime-mode Hamiltonian itself has conserved occupation numbers; a partition-function identity alone does not establish chaotic dynamics.

section: 13.3 When the uniform state is an attractor
text:
13.3 When the uniform state is an attractor
Let \(D\) be a \(d\times d\) doubly stochastic matrix and \(u_i=1/d\). Since its rows sum to one, \(Du=u\). Its columns summing to one ensure normalization of \(Dp\). These facts establish a stationary uniform state, but they do not establish attraction. The identity matrix preserves every distribution, and a cyclic permutation rotates distributions forever.
A sufficient condition is primitivity: for some integer \(m\), every entry of \(D^m\) is positive. Set \(a=\min_{ij}(D^m)_{ij}>0\) and \(\delta=da\leq1\). If \(\delta<1\), write
\[
D^m=\delta J+(1-\delta)R,\qquad J_{ij}=1/d,
\]
where \(R\) is again doubly stochastic and nonnegative. If \(\delta=1\), \(D^m=J\) and mixing is already exact. For any vector \(x\), column stochasticity and the triangle inequality give
\[
\norm{Rx}_1\leq\sum_{ij}R_{ij}|x_j|=\norm{x}_1.
\]
Because \(J(p-u)=0\),
\[
\norm{D^{mn}p-u}_1\leq(1-\delta)^n\norm{p-u}_1.
\tag{13.4}\]
Intermediate applications of \(D\) cannot increase this norm, so \(D^np\to u\). The bound is constructive, although often far from optimal. Spectrally, primitivity means that the eigenvalue one is simple and all other eigenvalues have modulus smaller than one. For a finite Markov chain it is equivalent to irreducibility plus aperiodicity. Reducible dynamics can retain independent conserved sectors, and a uniform state over the whole Hilbert space is then the wrong target. Time-dependent products require their own mixing conditions; primitivity of an unrelated average matrix is insufficient.

section: 13.4 A constructive proof of Birkhoff’s theorem
text:
13.4 A constructive proof of Birkhoff’s theorem
The theorem. Every finite doubly stochastic matrix is a convex combination of permutation matrices: \(D=\sum_a w_aP_a\), \(w_a\geq0\), \(\sum_aw_a=1\).
First regard the nonzero entries of \(D\) as edges of a bipartite graph connecting rows to columns. For a subset \(S\) of rows, let \(N(S)\) be the columns connected to them. Their total row weight is \(|S|\), and it all lies in \(N(S)\). The total weight in those columns is \(|N(S)|\), so \(|N(S)|\geq|S|\).
This condition guarantees a matching covering all rows. To see why, start with a matching of maximal size. If a row is unmatched, follow alternating paths: an unused edge from a row to a column, then the matching edge back to a row. If an unmatched column is reached, reversing the path increases the matching, contradicting maximality. Otherwise every reached column is matched to a reached row, while the initial unmatched row supplies one additional reached row. The reached rows then outnumber their neighboring columns, contradicting the condition above. Hence a perfect matching exists.
Choose its permutation matrix \(P\) and put \(w=\min_iD_{i,P(i)}>0\). Then \(D-wP\) is nonnegative with row and column sums \(1-w\). If \(w=1\) we are done. Otherwise
\[
D=wP+(1-w)D_1,\qquad D_1=\frac{D-wP}{1-w}
\]
and \(D_1\) is doubly stochastic. At least one previously positive entry has become zero, and no zero has become positive. Repeating the procedure must terminate after finitely many steps. Expanding the nested decompositions gives the desired positive weights, which sum to one.
For example, \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0.6&0.4\\0.4&0.6\end{smallmatrix}\right)=0.6I+0.4\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). This is an algebraic representation of population mixing. It does not assert that a particular unitary evolution physically tosses a classical coin between permutations. Quantum transition probabilities \(D_{ij}=|U_{ij}|^2\) form a subset of doubly stochastic matrices, and Birkhoff’s theorem applies to that subset as well.

text:
13.5 A rigorous passive-work inequality
Consider a cyclic process: the final Hamiltonian equals the initial one. Order its energies as \(E_1\leq\cdots\leq E_d\) and let the initial state be diagonal with \(p_1\geq\cdots\geq p_d\). Such a state is passive. A unitary process gives final energy populations \(q=Dp\), where \(D_{ij}=|U_{ij}|^2\) is doubly stochastic. We prove
\[
\ev W=\sum_iE_i(q_i-p_i)\geq0.
\tag{13.5}\]
For each \(k<d\), define \(r_j=\sum_{i\leq k}D_{ij}\). Then \(0\leq r_j\leq1\) and \(\sum_jr_j=k\). Since the \(p_j\) decrease with \(j\), the largest possible value of \(\sum_jr_jp_j\) is obtained by giving weight one to the first \(k\) entries. This can also be seen by repeatedly moving available weight from a larger index to a smaller one, which never lowers the sum. Therefore
\[
\sum_{i\leq k}q_i=\sum_jr_jp_j\leq\sum_{i\leq k}p_i.
\]
Set \(R_k=\sum_{i\leq k}(q_i-p_i)\leq0\), with \(R_0=R_d=0\). Discrete summation by parts yields
\[
\ev W=\sum_iE_i(R_i-R_{i-1})
=\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}(E_k-E_{k+1})R_k\geq0.
\]
Each factor in each product is nonpositive. No chaos assumption, large-system limit, or canonical ensemble was used. The proof works for every doubly stochastic population map. Degenerate energies cause no problem because the corresponding energy gaps vanish.
A Gibbs distribution with \(\beta\geq0\) is passive because its populations decrease with energy. Conversely, a population inversion \(p_j>p_i\) for \(E_j>E_i\) permits work extraction by swapping levels: the change is \((E_j-E_i)(p_i-p_j)<0\). Coherences also matter: a general passive state must commute with \(H\), since an appropriate unitary can otherwise lower its energy. With degeneracies one can diagonalize within each energy subspace.
Passivity for one copy is weaker than complete passivity, which requires that no number of copies allow work extraction by a joint cycle. The latter singles out equilibrium Gibbs states and ground-state cases under the appropriate hypotheses  [4,5]. For a noncyclic protocol with different initial and final spectra, Equation 13.5 is not the relevant comparison without additional terms.

text:
13.6 Deriving the energy drift–diffusion relation
Let \(P(E,t)\) be a density per unit energy and \(w(E,\omega)\dd\omega\) the rate for a jump from \(E\) to \(E+\omega\). The gain–loss equation is
\[
\partial_tP(E)=\int\dd\omega\,
\left[w(E-\omega,\omega)P(E-\omega)-w(E,\omega)P(E)\right].
\]
If jumps are small compared with the scale on which the distribution and rates vary, Taylor expansion of the gain term produces the first two Kramers–Moyal terms:
\[
\partial_tP=-\partial_E(AP)+\frac12\partial_E^2(BP),\qquad
A(E)=\int\dd\omega\,\omega w(E,\omega),\quad
B(E)=\int\dd\omega\,\omega^2w(E,\omega).
\tag{13.6}\]
\(A\) has units energy/time and \(B\) has units energy squared/time. On an infinitesimal interval they are the mean energy increment and its variance divided by elapsed time; the distinction between the second raw moment and variance is higher order in that interval. Neglecting third and higher jump moments needs a controlled small-jump regime, rather than an assumption that every finite-time work distribution is Gaussian.
Write the probability current as \(j=AP-\tfrac12\partial_E(BP)\). For energy-space evolution induced by a unital or doubly stochastic microscopic process at fixed Hamiltonian, the state uniform over individual levels is stationary. Its coarse-grained energy density is proportional to the density of levels \(\Omega(E)\), which is generally not constant. For a bounded spectrum with reflecting endpoints, the stationary current vanishes. Substituting \(P_{\infty}\propto\Omega\) gives
\[
2A=B\,\partial_E\ln\Omega+\partial_EB
=\beta(E)B+\partial_EB,
\qquad \beta(E)=\partial_ES(E),\quad
S(E)=\ln[\Omega(E)\delta E].
\tag{13.7}\]
The arbitrary fixed coarse-graining width \(\delta E\) drops out of \(\beta\). The derivative term is required for spatially varying diffusion in the Itô/Fokker–Planck convention used here. Dropping it is an additional slowly-varying-coefficient approximation. This argument uses stationarity and a zero-current boundary condition; a doubly stochastic matrix need not satisfy pairwise detailed balance.
For a system weakly coupled to a thermal reservoir at inverse temperature \(\beta_b\), the equilibrium energy density is \(\Omega(E)e^{-\beta_bE}\). The corresponding zero-current relation is \(2A=(\beta(E)-\beta_b)B+B'\). For two finite isolated subsystems exchanging energy, the stationary marginal is proportional to \(\Omega_1(E)\Omega_2(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-E)\), so the entropy gradient is \(\beta_1(E)-\beta_2(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-E)\). In the macroscopic limit, the drift therefore drives energy toward the subsystem of higher inverse temperature (the colder body), with the finite-size derivative term supplying the correction.
For several exchanged quantities \(x_i\), the same calculation gives
\[
A_i=\frac12\sum_j\left(B_{ij}\partial_{x_j}S+\partial_{x_j}B_{ij}\right)
\tag{13.8}\]
when the stationary diffusion has zero vector current. \(B_{ij}\) is a symmetric covariance-rate matrix. Nonzero circulation currents or time-reversal breaking require a more general treatment.

title: 13  Mathematical tools and two revealing examples
text:
13.7 Deriving Onsager reciprocity
Take two large bodies exchanging extensive quantities \(x_i\), each even under time reversal for the moment. Define the thermodynamic affinities \(F_i=\partial S_{\mathrm{tot}}/\partial x_i\), with \(x_i\) oriented into the first body. For energy exchange \(F_E=\beta_1-\beta_2\). A microscopic reversibility relation for an exchange \(\Delta x\) over a mesoscopic interval \(\tau\) has the near-equilibrium form
\[
\frac{p_F(\Delta x)}{p_F(-\Delta x)}
=e^{F\cdot\Delta x},
\]
when the reversed experiment coincides with the forward one, affinities vary negligibly during the interval, and the coarse-grained exchange description is valid. At equilibrium \(p_0(\Delta x)=p_0(-\Delta x)\). Linearizing the ratio gives \(p_F(\Delta x)-p_F(-\Delta x)=p_0(\Delta x)\sum_jF_j\Delta x_j+O(F^2)\). Hence
\[
J_i\equiv\frac{\ev{\Delta x_i}}{\tau}
=\sum_jL_{ij}F_j+O(F^2),\qquad
L_{ij}=\frac{\ev{\Delta x_i\Delta x_j}_0}{2\tau}.
\tag{13.9}\]
The symmetry \(L_{ij}=L_{ji}\) follows from the symmetry of a covariance. Positivity also follows: for real \(v_i\), \(v_iL_{ij}v_j=\ev{(v\cdot\Delta x)^2}_0/(2\tau)\geq0\). Thus entropy production \(\dot S=F\cdot J=F^{\mathsf T}LF\) is nonnegative to quadratic order. Reciprocity constrains cross effects, for example the relation between heat transport induced by a particle affinity and particle transport induced by a temperature affinity. It is the content of microscopic reversibility beyond a mere positivity condition  [6].
There is a useful Green–Kubo version. For classical equilibrium currents, \(\Delta x_i=\int_0^\tau I_i(t)\dd t\). If their correlations decay and \(\tau\) is long compared with that decay time but short compared with the relaxation of the bodies, stationarity gives
\[
L_{ij}=\frac12\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dd t\,
\ev{I_i(t)I_j(0)}_{\mathrm{eq}}.
\]
For equal time-reversal parities, reversibility converts this into the familiar integral over positive times. In a quantum calculation the linear-response version uses the canonical Kubo correlation, with imaginary-time averaging, rather than assuming that noncommuting current products are classical random variables. In a thermal state it can be written \(\langle A;B\rangle_{\mathrm{eq}}=\beta^{-1}\int_0^\beta\dd\lambda\,\tr[\rho_{\mathrm{eq}}e^{\lambda H}Ae^{-\lambda H}B]\) for zero-mean operators. Forces must be normalized as entropy affinities, as above, to compare prefactors.
If a magnetic field \(B_{\mathrm{mag}}\) or another time-reversal-odd control is present, reversal changes that control too. If variable \(x_i\) has time-reversal parity \(\varepsilon_i\), the appropriate relation is Onsager–Casimir reciprocity, \(L_{ij}(B_{\mathrm{mag}})=\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_jL_{ji}(-B_{\mathrm{mag}})\). Symmetry at the same field is then not generally required. Ballistic currents or additional conserved quantities can prevent the correlation integral from converging to a finite diffusive coefficient. Far from equilibrium, derivatives of the covariance and higher cumulants enter; the linear relation proved here should not be asserted unchanged.

title: 13  Mathematical tools and two revealing examples
text:
13.8 Exercises and worked answers

Area preservation. Compute the determinant of the standard map’s tangent matrix. Does this rule out exponential separation?
Answer. The determinant is \(1+K\cos\theta-K\cos\theta=1\). One expanding tangent direction can coexist with one contracting direction, keeping their area product fixed. Volume preservation is compatible with chaos.
A mixing counterexample. The matrix \(D=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) is doubly stochastic and irreducible. Why does it not approach the uniform state?
Answer. It has period two, \(D^2=I\), and an eigenvalue \(-1\). No power has all positive entries, so it is not primitive. A distribution \((p,1-p)\) alternates with \((1-p,p)\).
Compute passive work. Let \(E=(0,1,3)\) and \(p=(0.6,0.3,0.1)\). A unitary swaps the first and last levels. Find the work.
Answer. The final populations are \((0.1,0.3,0.6)\). The initial energy is \(0.6\) and the final energy \(2.1\), so \(\ev W=1.5\). The swap supplies energy to the system, as passivity requires.
Check a diffusion law. Suppose \(\Omega(E)\propto E^\alpha\) and \(B(E)=bE^r\) on a positive-energy interval. Find the zero-current drift.
Answer. \(\beta(E)=\alpha/E\), so Equation 13.7 gives \(A(E)=b(\alpha+r)E^{r-1}/2\). Both the state-counting contribution \(\alpha\) and the diffusion-gradient contribution \(r\) matter. Boundary conditions and validity of the small-jump approximation still have to be supplied.
Reciprocity versus positivity. Does positive entropy production by itself imply \(L_{12}=L_{21}\)?
Answer. No. \(F^{\mathsf T}LF\) depends only on the symmetric part of \(L\). An antisymmetric part contributes zero to entropy production. Reciprocity needs microscopic reversibility and the appropriate parity/field reversal, not positivity alone.

[2] H. L. Montgomery, The Pair Correlation of Zeros of the Zeta Function, in Analytic Number Theory, edited by H. G. Diamond, Vol. 24 (American Mathematical Society, 1973), pp. 181–193.


[3] A. M. Odlyzko, On the distribution of spacings between zeros of the zeta function, Mathematics of Computation 48, 273 (1987).


[4] A. Lenard, Thermodynamical proof of the gibbs formula for elementary quantum systems, Journal of Statistical Physics 19, 575 (1978).


[5] W. Pusz and S. L. Woronowicz, Passive states and KMS states for general quantum systems, Communications in Mathematical Physics 58, 273 (1978).


[6] L. Onsager, Reciprocal relations in irreversible processes. I., Physical Review 37, 405 (1931).

section: 14.2 Experiment 1: level statistics with a known ensemble
text:
14.2 Experiment 1: level statistics with a known ensemble
Start with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble, so the statistical model is specified independently of any many-body conjecture. Draw a real matrix \(X\) with independent standard normal entries and set
\[
H=\frac{X+X^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{2D}},\qquad D=350.
\tag{14.1}\]
Its off-diagonal variance is \(1/D\) and its diagonal variance is \(2/D\). At large \(D\) its mean density has the semicircle form
\[
\rho(E)=\frac{D}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-E^2},\qquad |E|<2.
\]
Unfolding transforms energy to mean level count. An antiderivative of the normalized density is
\[
F(E)=\frac12+\frac1\pi\left[\arcsin\frac E2+
\frac E4\sqrt{4-E^2}\right].
\]
Check this by differentiation: the two derivative terms combine to \(\sqrt{4-E^2}/(2\pi)\). Define unfolded coordinates \(x_n=DF(E_n)\) and spacings \(s_n=x_{n+1}-x_n\). The calculation retains eigenvalues 71 through 280 in each of 25 matrices, avoiding the spectral edges, and normalizes the pooled spacings to mean one. This ensemble-density unfolding is appropriate because the ensemble is known. An arbitrary spin chain generally needs its own smooth counting function or an unfolding-free statistic.
The comparison sample consists of independent unit-mean exponential random numbers. That is the exact nearest-neighbor spacing law for a homogeneous Poisson point process. No matrix diagonalization is needed to generate this benchmark. The spacing data include both samples.
The GOE Wigner surmise, \(P(s)=(\pi s/2)e^{-\pi s^2/4}\), is exact for a suitably normalized two-level model and an excellent approximation to bulk large-GOE spacings. It is not the exact large-\(D\) distribution. The suppression at \(s=0\) is the useful qualitative distinction from \(e^{-s}\).
Checkpoint. Plot the ratio \(r_n=\min(s_n,s_{n+1})/\max(s_n,s_{n+1})\). Avoid forming a ratio across the boundary between two independent matrix samples; the checked-in pooled file is intended for the spacing histogram. For a new ratio calculation, keep each spectrum separate.
Worked answer. Form diff(E) within each retained spectrum, then compute neighboring ratios before pooling. A slowly varying local density approximately cancels. The Poisson mean is \(2\ln2-1\), obtained by integrating \(r\) against \(2/(1+r)^2\) on \([0,1]\). Ratios reduce unfolding sensitivity but still require symmetry resolution in a physical Hamiltonian.

title: 14  A reproducible numerical laboratory
section: 14.3 Experiment 2: exact dynamics of a small spin chain
text:
14.3 Experiment 2: exact dynamics of a small spin chain
We use an open chain with \(L=9\) spin-\(1/2\) sites and \(D=512\) states,
\[
H=-\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}Z_iZ_{i+1}
-1.05\sum_{i=1}^L X_i
-\sum_{i=1}^L(0.35+0.07i)Z_i.
\tag{14.2}\]
Here \(X,Z\) are Pauli matrices, not spin operators \(\sigma/2\). Energies are in units of the Ising coupling and times in its inverse with \(\hbar=1\). The longitudinal field breaks the global spin flip, its spatial variation breaks reflection, and the transverse field mixes magnetization sectors. The model is real, so its remaining antiunitary symmetry is ordinary complex conjugation. These observations make the example useful for studying a generic finite chain; they do not prove chaos or ETH in an infinite system.
A computational state is an integer \(s=0,\ldots,2^L-1\). Site 1 is the least significant bit. A zero bit has \(Z=+1\), a one bit \(Z=-1\), and \(X_i\) flips bit \(i-1\). Thus the off-diagonal entry is H[xor(s, 1 << (i-1)) + 1, s+1] = -1.05. The extra one converts zero-based bit labels to Julia array indices. All \(ZZ\) and longitudinal-field terms are diagonal. This construction needs no tensor-library convention.
The observable is \(A=Z_5\). Among computational states with \(Z_5=+1\), choose the one whose diagonal energy is nearest the mean eigenenergy. This deterministic rule selects a nonstationary product state with energy in the central region. It is a sudden preparation in the final Hamiltonian, equivalently a quench from a strong pinning Hamiltonian whose product ground state is the chosen configuration. The initial energy width remains finite; no narrow-shell limit is presumed.
Diagonalize \(H=V\operatorname{diag}(E_n)V^{\dagger}\). If the chosen initial basis index is \(j\), then \(c_n=V_{jn}^{*}\). In this real model conjugation changes nothing, but it matters for complex Hamiltonians. Compute
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{nn}&=\sum_s Z_5(s)|V_{sn}|^2,\\
\psi_s(t)&=\sum_n V_{sn}c_ne^{-iE_nt},\\
A(t)&=\sum_s Z_5(s)|\psi_s(t)|^2,\\
A_{\mathrm{DE}}&=\sum_n |c_n|^2A_{nn}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.3}\]
The comparison microcanonical value is an unweighted average over \(|E_n-E_0|<0.8\), with \(E_0=\sum_n|c_n|^2E_n\). Its window is an explicit finite-size choice. A better comparison study varies that width and system size instead of choosing a window after looking at agreement.






Figure 14.1: Independent finite-chain illustration: diagonal matrix elements of the central spin and exact product-state dynamics under the Hamiltonian specified in the text. The lines compare unitary dynamics, the diagonal ensemble, and an energy-window ensemble.



The raw eigenstate table contains energies, diagonal observable values, and initial probabilities; the time series contains the dynamics. The diagnostic file reports the chosen bit state, shell count, energy width, effective dimension \(d_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/\sum_n p_n^2\), and the gap-nondegeneracy expression for the long-time variance. The code does not certify that all energy gaps are nondegenerate; that expression is identified by its assumption.
The script checks Hermiticity, the eigensystem residual, normalization, agreement of the energy computed in both bases, and \(A(0)=1\). These checks catch basis, eigenvector, and propagation errors independently of whether the dynamics look thermal.
Checkpoint. Why can the diagonal and microcanonical lines differ even when the eigenstate scatter is fairly smooth?
Worked answer. The diagonal ensemble weights the full energy distribution \(p_n\), while the microcanonical average uses a particular shell. If the smooth curve \(a(E)\) bends across the initial distribution, then \(\sum_n p_na(E_n)-a(E_0)\simeq a''(E_0)\sigma_E^2/2\). Finite eigenstate fluctuations and finite shell sampling add other errors. A broad distribution or a spectral-edge state need not be represented by a single temperature.

title: 14  A reproducible numerical laboratory
text:
14.4 Experiment 3: classical phase-space structure
The script iterates the standard map
\[
p_{n+1}=p_n+K\sin\theta_n\pmod{2\pi},\qquad
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+p_{n+1}\pmod{2\pi}.
\]
Nine initial points are evolved for 1,800 steps at \(K=0.2\) and \(K=5\). The angle-momentum area is preserved: the kick and free-drift Jacobians each have determinant one. Putting momentum on a torus makes the plot compact; a physical kicked rotor can instead have unbounded momentum on a cylinder. Diffusion on that cylinder cannot be measured from momentum reduced modulo \(2\pi\).
Invariant curves, resonant islands, and broad chaotic regions can coexist. Visual coverage of a region by finitely many iterates does not prove ergodicity. To estimate a Lyapunov exponent, evolve a tangent vector with the map Jacobian, periodically renormalize it, and accumulate the logarithms of its growth factors. Compare trajectories started in different visible regions.
Worked extension. In the order \((\theta,p)\) the Jacobian is
\[
M_n=\begin{pmatrix}1+K\cos\theta_n&1\\K\cos\theta_n&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det M_n=1.
\]
With \(v_{n+1}=M_nv_n\), record \(\ell_n=\ln\norm{v_{n+1}}\), rescale to unit norm, and estimate \(\lambda=\sum_n\ell_n/n\). Discard a transient and vary both trajectory length and initial conditions. Positive finite-time growth is a numerical diagnostic, not a proof that every trajectory is chaotic.

title: 14  A reproducible numerical laboratory
section: 14.5 Experiment 4: distributions from a continuum model
text:
14.5 Experiment 4: distributions from a continuum model
The heating figure in Chapter 10 illustrates a specified Fokker–Planck model and an equilibrium sharing law. It does not simulate wall collisions. For the first panel choose \(S(E)=\tfrac12\ln E\), \(B(E)=E^{3/2}\), and \(A(E)=\sqrt E\), satisfying \(2A=B\partial_ES+\partial_EB\). In the equivalent Itô equation,
\[
\dd E=\sqrt E\,\dd t+E^{3/4}\dd W_t.
\]
Itô’s rule with \(x=\sqrt E\) gives
\[
\dd x=\frac38\dd t+\frac12\sqrt x\,\dd W_t.
\]
The entrance-law solution from \(x=0\) is a gamma density of shape 3 and scale \(t/8\). Transforming back produces
\[
P(E,t)=\frac{\sqrt E}{4(t/8)^3}e^{-8\sqrt E/t},\qquad E>0.
\]
Normalization follows by \(E=x^2\), \(\dd E=2x\dd x\): the integral becomes the normalized gamma integral. Its mean is \(\ev E=3\cdot4(t/8)^2\). The continuum law becomes questionable near energies comparable to the microscopic driving scale; its entrance solution is a mathematical similarity profile that illustrates late-time scaling, rather than a microscopic derivation for a particle initially at rest.
The second panel takes densities of states \(\Omega_1(E)\propto E^2\) and \(\Omega_2(E)\propto E^2\). At fixed total energy, \(u=E_1/E_{\mathrm{tot}}\) has \(P(u)=30u^2(1-u)^2\). Integrating the polynomial proves normalization; symmetry gives \(\ev u=1/2\). The sharing table permits a direct numerical check. Equal mean energy here follows from choosing identical densities of states. In general equilibrium equalizes inverse temperature.

title: 14  A reproducible numerical laboratory
section: 14.6 A project that tests a claim
text:
14.6 A project that tests a claim
Extend the spin-chain calculation to \(L=7,8,9,10\) and compare the central part of the spectrum. Specify the window and statistic before examining the result. One useful quantity is the variance of \(A_{nn}\) after subtracting a local smooth energy trend. Track the maximum deviation separately from the average deviation: these address different strengths of ETH. Another is the scale of off-diagonal matrix elements inside a narrow mean-energy bin, resolved by frequency.
Dense exact diagonalization uses memory of order \(D^2=4^L\) and work of order \(D^3\). Doubling a visible chain length is therefore far more expensive than doubling an ordinary array. Keep the first project small, preserve the data, and state the accessible sizes. A careful finite-size conclusion is more informative than an unsupported assertion of universal thermalization.
